About this book. I wrote this as a free, evidence-based companion to the System of Inevitability, which I created and have developed over more than twenty-five years. Descriptions of the System are my own. Where this book suggests progressions, tests, or safety rules, those are my suggestions based on the general scientific literature, not a formal syllabus.

Health notice. This book is for education and inspiration. It is not medical advice and does not replace a physician, physiotherapist, or qualified coach. Heavy implements thrown, caught, and spun near your face, wrists, shoulders, and spine can injure you. Consult a qualified professional before starting, especially if you are pregnant, have a heart, joint, bone, eye, or balance condition, are recovering from injury, or are new to exercise. You train at your own risk.

About the science. Every study cited here was checked against its published record (authors, year, journal, and DOI) at the time of writing. No study, number, or quotation has been invented. Where the evidence is thin, the text says so.

Dedication

For everyone who has ever dropped the ball and bent down to pick it up again.

And for the stonemasons, the street jugglers, and the quiet practitioners in garages and backyards who keep the old conversation between body and world alive.

How to Read This Book

This book makes a promise to you: it will tell you, at every important turn, how sure we are.

Science is not a pile of facts. It is a set of claims held with different degrees of confidence. Some findings have been replicated across thousands of people on several continents. Some rest on a single small, clever experiment. Some are honest hypotheses still waiting for their test. And some things in this book are not science at all. They are the lived experience and philosophy of a practitioner, which has its own kind of value and should be honored as that, not dressed up as a laboratory result.

So you will see three kinds of marked boxes:

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established. Supported by multiple independent studies, systematic reviews, or meta-analyses with reasonably consistent results. You can lean on these.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Suggestive or emerging. Supported by real peer-reviewed research, but the studies are few, small, short, indirect, or debated. Promising, but hold them loosely.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Practitioner experience and philosophy. Ideas, claims, or experiences from the System of Inevitability or from contemplative and martial traditions that have not been directly measured. They may be true and useful. They have not been tested.

There is a fourth kind of box, which you should never skip:

⚠ Caution

Caution. Practical safety information. Heavy objects are honest teachers, and they do not negotiate.

Citations appear in the text as author and year, for example (Draganski et al., 2004). The full list, with journal details and DOIs, is in the References at the back. If a sentence makes a factual claim about the world and has no citation and no box, treat it as my reasonable summary or opinion.

One more thing. The phrase upgrade in human consciousness appears in this book because it names a real hope: that ordinary people, through patient practice, can become more awake, more present, more skillful, and kinder to one another. This book treats that hope as an inspirational theme rooted in what is actually known about attention, learning, the plastic brain, and flow. It does not claim that juggling iron balls or spinning a ring on a bar has been shown to alter consciousness in any metaphysical sense. That is not a lesser claim. It is an honest one, and honesty is the ground everything else in this book stands on.

Foreword

“Training method is just walking and turning.” — from the System of Inevitability project materials

I built this practice over more than twenty-five years, out of the most basic human movements.

There are three iron balls, each weighing six pounds, kept in the air in the oldest patterns in juggling. There is a five-foot stainless-steel bar weighing twenty-five pounds, held palms-down, with a small iron ring spinning around it, kept centered and spinning in both directions while the body walks and turns. There is a heavy bag and a wooden-dummy-style training post with metal arms. There is a philosophy that fits in a sentence: training method is just walking and turning. And there is a refusal of the usual scaffolding: no instructors, no belts.

What matters to me is not the spectacle, though it is a spectacle. It is the idea underneath it. I spent twenty-five years building a practice out of walking, turning, catching, releasing, and made those movements so demanding that they require total attention. It looks like strength training. It also looks like meditation. It looks like a body thinking.

I wanted to know what science could honestly say about that. Not to debunk it and not to sell it, but to understand it. What happens in a brain that learns to juggle? What happens in a tendon that is loaded for decades? Why does grip strength predict how long people live? What is flow, and is it real? Can attention be trained, and does it change who we are? And what happens when one person’s private practice is given away freely to anyone who wants it?

This book is my attempt to answer those questions as carefully as I can, and then to hand the answers to you for free.

You will find inspiration here, because the science of human learning is genuinely inspiring. The adult brain changes measurably when it learns something new. Older adults learn new motor skills. Strength protects us. Attention can be cultivated, and a wandering mind tends to be an unhappy one. These are not slogans. They are findings.

You will also find restraint, because inspiration that outruns the evidence eventually betrays the people it inspires. Some of the claims made for heavy juggling and spinning bars have not been tested. Some of the loads involved are genuinely dangerous for beginners. I have tried to mark every one of those places clearly, and to offer a gentler, safer road in.

If this book does its job, you will finish it wanting to practice: to pick up three soft balls, or a broomstick, or simply to walk and turn with more attention than you did yesterday. And then, I hope, you will give it to someone else.

— Cory Snell

Part I · The Way

Walking. Turning. Catching what falls and sending it back up. The oldest movements, made new by attention.

An Invitation to Practice

Chapter 1

“No instructors required. No belts. Just the tools, the physics, and the will to train.” — System of Inevitability, public statement

Pick up a ball and toss it from one hand to the other.

That is all. Nothing remarkable happened. And yet, in the half-second the ball was in the air, an astonishing amount of work took place. Your eyes caught the ball as it left your fingers and estimated its arc. Your brain predicted where it would come down, long before it arrived, and moved your other hand to meet it. Muscles in your forearm, shoulder, and trunk adjusted for its weight. Sensors in your skin, joints, and muscles reported the catch, and your nervous system compared what happened with what it expected. If the toss went slightly wrong, you corrected without thinking. If it went badly wrong, you laughed, or swore, and tried again.

Now imagine three balls instead of one, so that one is always in the air. Now imagine those balls are made of iron and weigh six pounds each. Now imagine doing it for twenty-five years.

This book is about a practice built on that idea, and about the science of what happens to a human being who commits to it. Not just to the muscles, though they matter, but to the brain that learns, the tendons that adapt, the attention that narrows and deepens, and the inner life that changes when a person spends hours each week doing something difficult, rhythmic, and wholly absorbing.

A practice, not a product

The System of Inevitability is emergent, free-form body expression with no set form, developed over more than twenty-five years. The practice of iron ball juggling, the bar and spinning ring, the isometric push/pull with the ring, non-repetitive kinetic chaining on the bag, and work on the iron-armed dummy is a conceptual adjective that can be incorporated into any other system, anywhere, by anyone. It does not claim superiority. It is my interpretation and expression of the way of nature, based on the events of my life, my physical abilities according to my strengths and weaknesses, and an independent course of practice and self-discovery over the years, and nothing more. I am a stonemason and martial artist. The System has no ranks, no instructors, and no formal syllabus. Its tools are few and heavy: three iron balls juggled in classic patterns, a long steel bar with a spinning iron ring, a heavy bag, and a metal-armed training dummy in the Wing Chun tradition. Its philosophy is spare: natural body movements, geometric pathways, continuous motion, spirals felt in the body. Training method is just walking and turning.

You do not need to adopt this system to benefit from this book. You may never lift a six-pound iron ball, and if you are new to training you probably should not for a long time. But the principles underneath the System of Inevitability touch some of the most robust and hopeful findings in modern science:

  • The adult human brain physically changes when it learns a new skill, and juggling is the very skill that first showed this in humans (Draganski et al., 2004).
  • That capacity does not vanish with age. Older adults learn new motor skills, and their brains change too (Boyke et al., 2008; Voelcker-Rehage & Willimczik, 2006).
  • Muscular strength, and grip strength in particular, is one of the most consistent predictors of long-term health and survival ever measured (Leong et al., 2015; Celis-Morales et al., 2018).
  • Tendons adapt to load, slowly, when load is applied intelligently (Bohm et al., 2015).
  • Physical activity reliably improves mood and reduces symptoms of depression and anxiety (Singh et al., 2023; Noetel et al., 2024).
  • A mind absorbed in what it is doing tends to be happier than a mind wandering elsewhere (Killingsworth & Gilbert, 2010).

None of those findings is about iron balls. All of them are about the kind of human being that a patient, attentive, physically demanding practice might help you become.

The adult brain is not a finished building. It is a workshop that stays open.

What this book is, and what it is not

This book is three things at once.

It is a portrait of a practice: what the System of Inevitability is, as I have described it and as I practise it, and what ideas animate it.

It is a review of the science that bears on that practice, written for curious non-specialists. That science is real, peer-reviewed, and checked. It is also, in places, incomplete, and you will be told where.

And it is an invitation: a suggested, safe path that lets almost anyone begin a version of this practice with light tools, simple tests, and clear rules for when to stop.

It is not a formal syllabus, because this practice has no written syllabus. The progressions in Chapter 12 are suggestions drawn from general exercise science.

It is also not a claim that this practice will make you a better fighter, a more enlightened person, or a different species. Some of the strongest claims made for heavy juggling and rotational bar work, especially that they transfer automatically to fighting skill, have never been measured. This book will tell you where those claims stand: asserted, plausible in part, untested.

Why “consciousness”?

The person who asked for this book wanted it to help “facilitate an upgrade in human consciousness.” That is a large phrase, and it deserves a careful answer.

Science does not have a settled theory of consciousness, and nothing in this book proves that any practice changes consciousness in a deep metaphysical sense. But science does have a great deal to say about things that are very close to what most people mean by the phrase:

  • Attention: what we notice, how long we can hold it, and how it can be trained.
  • Awareness of the body: proprioception (the sense of where your body is) and interoception (the sense of what is happening inside it).
  • Plasticity: the brain’s capacity to rewire itself through experience.
  • Flow: the state of total absorption in a challenging activity, where self-consciousness fades and action seems to happen by itself.
  • Wellbeing: mood, anxiety, resilience, and the sense that life is meaningful.
  • Connection: how shared practice and moving together affect how we feel about one another.

If an “upgrade in consciousness” means becoming more attentive, more present in the body, more capable of learning, more often absorbed and less often anxious, and more connected to others, then there is real evidence that practice can move us in that direction. That is the sense in which this book uses the phrase. It is an inspiration grounded in evidence, not a promise beyond it.

How the book is organized

Part I, The Way, introduces the System of Inevitability and its philosophy.

Part II, The Tools, takes each implement in turn, the iron balls, the spinning ring bar, and the contact tools of bag and dummy, and asks what the science says about each.

Part III, The Science, steps back to the big themes: the brain that learns, how skill is built, the body that adapts, attention and flow, and movement and mood.

Part IV, The Spiral Outward, asks what happens when a solitary practice is shared: community without hierarchy, a safe path for beginners, and a closing invitation.

At the back you will find practice logs you can copy, a glossary, and a complete list of references.

Start wherever you like. But if you intend to train, please read Chapter 12 before you pick up anything heavy.

The Stonemason’s Method

Chapter 2

Continuous motion is geometry, not style. — paraphrasing a theme of the System of Inevitability project visuals

Every practice carries the fingerprints of the life that made it. To understand the System of Inevitability, it helps to begin not with the iron balls but with the stone.

Hands that learned from stone

By my own public account, I have spent more than twenty-five years as a stonemason and martial artist. I juggled on the street in the 1990s. Over the decades I refined a practice largely alone, and I describe every part of my life as interdependent with it: the work, the training, the tools.

Consider for a moment what stonemasonry asks of a body. Stone is heavy, irregular, and unforgiving. It must be lifted, turned, set, and adjusted, day after day, often with the hands in awkward positions. A mason’s grip is not the grip of a gym, where bars are knurled and loads are symmetrical. It is the grip of a person holding an object that wants to slip, roll, and fall. It is endurance strength more than peak strength: hours of holding, carrying, rotating, and placing.

The System of Inevitability’s materials occasionally point to this occupational loading as the base on which the training tools sit. That is an important and honest detail. The iron balls and the twenty-five-pound bar were not dropped onto an untrained body. They were added, over years, to a body already adapted by decades of manual work. As we will see in Chapter 8, tendons and connective tissues adapt slowly, and the loads that are safe for a long-adapted body can be dangerous for an untrained one.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Practitioner experience. The idea that stonemasonry provided a foundation of grip and tendon tolerance is my own account of my history. It is entirely plausible given what is known about tissue adaptation to long-term loading (see Chapter 8), but it has not been measured in my case.

The tools, as publicly described

On 30 July 2026, I publicly described the core tools of the system. They are summarized here as I presented them. The claimed benefits are mine, and are listed as claims.

1. Iron ball juggling

Three metal balls of 6 lb (about 2.7 kg) each, worked in three classic juggling patterns:

  • The Cascade, the basic three-ball pattern, in which each ball is thrown from one hand in an arc to the other, tracing a figure-eight in the air.
  • Mills Mess, a pattern in which the arms continuously cross and uncross, so that balls are thrown and caught in a weaving, spiraling motion.
  • The Box, a pattern in which two balls rise and fall vertically on either side while a third is passed horizontally between the hands, so that the pattern traces a rectangle.

Claimed benefits, as stated: continuous regenerative power (absorbing force on the catch and reversing it into the next throw), multi-plane torque, predictive tracking of multiple objects, grip endurance, core linking, and structural integrity under dynamic load. In a follow-up post on 31 July 2026, these benefits were asserted to transfer to striking (“chamber-to-impact without energy leakage”), blocking (“receive and redirect force”), clinch, trapping, and awareness of multiple threats.

2. The Spinning Ring Iron Bar

A five-foot, 25 lb stainless-steel bar held palms-down. Around it, a 6-inch, 2 lb iron ring is kept continuously spinning and centered, in both directions. The bar is worked overhead, at roughly 45 degrees with a back-bend, or projected from the chest, either standing still or moving.

Claimed benefits, as stated: grip, forearm, and wrist resilience; rotator cuff and scapular stability; rotational core power; proprioceptive acuity; and tendon durability under persistent multi-planar instability.

3. Overlay tools

A heavy bag and a custom metal-armed training dummy (built from schedule-40 pipe) in the Wing Chun tradition. These are used for contact skill and structure: the part of training in which force actually meets resistance.

The philosophy: walking and turning

What unites these tools is not their weight but a way of seeing movement. The system’s public materials express it in a few phrases:

  • “Training method is just walking and turning.”
  • Natural body movements, geometric pathways, and heavy iron conditioning tools.
  • Continuous motion and geometry felt in the body: spirals, regenerative torque, kinetic chaining.
  • Low-impact, high-control, and scalable for serious practitioners of any age; no hierarchy or competition required.
  • “No instructors required. No belts. Just the tools, the physics, and the will to train.”

There is something quietly radical in “walking and turning.” It locates the source of skill not in secret techniques but in the two most universal human movements. Every person who can walk has a gait cycle, a rhythm of loading and unloading, falling and catching. Every person who can turn has a spiral available in the hips, spine, and shoulders. The system’s claim, as a philosophy, is that these ordinary movements, refined under load and attention, contain everything needed.

Some of the system’s visuals also show spirals as something revealed in practice, and occasionally use natural, flowing, even psychedelic imagery. These images express how the practice feels from the inside: continuous, geometric, alive.

The claim is not that the body needs secret techniques. It is that ordinary movements, refined under load and attention, contain everything.

Reading the philosophy carefully

It would be easy to read this philosophy either too literally or too cynically. Neither helps.

Read too literally, “any age” and “low-impact” could suggest that a beginner of seventy can pick up three six-pound iron balls tomorrow. That would be dangerous. A dropped six-pound ball is not low-impact for a foot, a wrist, or a face. A 25 lb bar held at 45 degrees in a back-bend places real demands on the lower back and shoulders. These loads are scalable only if there is a scale: a progression that begins far lighter. The system’s public materials do not yet include that progression. Chapter 12 offers one, clearly labeled as a suggestion.

Read too cynically, the philosophy could be dismissed as poetry. That would miss something real. As we will see, there is genuine science behind the idea that continuous, absorbing, whole-body skill practice changes the brain, strengthens the body, and steadies the mind. The philosophy points at real phenomena even where its specific claims run ahead of the measurements.

The most respectful reading is a precise one: honor the practice, take its experience seriously, and test its claims.

An honest assessment

In October 2026, a viability assessment was filed on the system as part of the project that led to this book. Its conclusions are worth stating plainly, because they shape everything that follows.

What holds. Ordinary juggling produces measurable, if temporary, changes in brain regions that process visual motion (Draganski et al., 2004). Rotational implements in the mace and club family have, in at least one recent randomized trial, improved grip strength, shoulder flexibility, and closed-chain upper-body stability (Akaras et al., 2026). Decades of stonemasonry and contact work provide a credible base for grip, tendon tolerance, and contact skill.

What does not hold, yet. The juggling brain studies used ordinary, light balls and a cascade of about a minute. Six-pound iron balls, roughly twenty times the weight of a typical juggling ball, are a different stimulus that has never been studied. Mace and club trials are not direct evidence for a spinning ring on a bar. “Low-impact” and “any age” are in tension with the actual loads. And the transfer of these skills to clinch, striking, and multi-threat awareness is asserted, not measured: there are no recorded bouts, force measurements, or independent practitioners on record.

What would make it viable as a system that other people could learn safely: a written progression from light tools to heavy ones, with clear stop rules; a few simple, repeatable tests; filmed standards and an injury log; and a clean separation between training-method claims and unproven martial or metaphysical ones.

The assessment’s verdict was this: conditionally viable as a personal conditioning practice for an already-adapted practitioner; not yet viable as a transmissible martial system.

This book takes that verdict not as a dismissal but as a map. Everything it lists as missing, a progression, tests, logs, and a separation of claims, this book tries to supply in draft form, so that anyone who is inspired can begin safely, and so that the practice can grow into something others can test, share, and improve.

Inevitability

A last word about the name. “Inevitable” can sound like a boast. In the context of training, it has a gentler and more interesting meaning.

When you juggle well, the next throw is inevitable. It is already contained in the catch. The ball arrives; the hand gives with it, absorbing its momentum; and that same yielding motion becomes the beginning of the next throw. Nothing is forced. Each action follows from the one before it, the way each step of walking follows from the fall of the one before.

That is what continuous regenerative power means as a felt experience: not a bigger force, but a movement with no wasted beginnings. The catch becomes the throw. The turn becomes the walk. The end of one thing is the start of the next.

Whether or not that experience transfers to fighting, it is a beautiful thing to feel. And as we will see, the conditions that produce it, challenge matched to skill, total attention, immediate feedback, are exactly the conditions that psychologists associate with flow.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

A note on other uses of “inevitable.” Some of my public posts use the word “inevitable” for political or metaphysical forecasts. Those posts are separate from the training method, and nothing in them is evidence for or against it. This book concerns itself only with the practice.

Iron Balls: The Art of the Cascade

Chapter 3

The catch becomes the throw.

Juggling is one of the oldest recorded human skills. It is also, by a happy accident of history, the skill that opened a new chapter in neuroscience. Before we come to the iron, we should understand the pattern.

Anatomy of a cascade

In the three-ball cascade, each hand throws a ball in an arc to the opposite hand, and the throws alternate: right, left, right, left. Because there are three balls and only two hands, one ball is always in the air. Each ball travels an arc that crosses the midline, and over time the three paths together trace a sideways figure-eight, a lemniscate, in the air in front of the juggler.

Juggling has been studied as a model of rhythmic coordination for decades. In a classic analysis, Beek and Turvey (1992) examined the temporal patterning of cascade juggling: how the time a ball spends in the hand relates to the time it spends in flight, and how jugglers keep these intervals stable while still adapting them. Their work showed that a skilled cascade is not a rigid clock but a flexibly coupled rhythm, in which hands and balls settle into stable timing relationships while retaining room to adjust.

Where do jugglers look? Huys and Beek (2002) recorded the gaze of intermediate and expert jugglers. Experts made smaller eye movements than intermediates, relative to the size of the pattern. They tracked each ball less, and seemed to rely more on glimpses of the balls near the tops of their arcs, letting the rest of the pattern be handled by prediction and by feel. In their words, expertise was “reflected by an overall reduction in the extent to which the balls are visually tracked.”

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established (for ordinary juggling). Skilled juggling relies on stable, flexibly coupled timing between hands and balls (Beek & Turvey, 1992), and expertise is associated with less visual tracking of each ball, not more (Huys & Beek, 2002). Skill shifts work from the eyes to prediction.

That shift, from watching everything to sensing the whole, will come up again and again in this book. It is what happens to attention when skill matures.

The three patterns of the System

The System of Inevitability names three patterns. Each asks something slightly different of the body.

The Cascade is the foundation: symmetrical, alternating, endlessly repeatable. Its demand is rhythm. In ordinary juggling it is the first pattern anyone learns, and it is the pattern used in the brain-imaging studies described below.

Mills Mess is a cascade in which the arms continuously cross over and under one another, so that each throw is made from a crossed or uncrossed position. To an onlooker the balls seem to weave around each other. To the juggler, the pattern demands rotation through the shoulders and forearms and an unusually rich sense of where each hand is in space. It is a pattern of spirals.

The Box breaks the cascade’s symmetry. Two balls are thrown straight up, one on each side, while the third is passed horizontally between the hands. The result is a rectangular pattern, with a distinct vertical rhythm on each side and a horizontal exchange through the middle. Its demand is coordination of two different kinds of throw at once.

Taken together, the three patterns train rhythm (Cascade), rotation (Mills Mess), and asymmetry (Box). In motor-learning terms, practicing several related variations rather than a single pattern is also a form of variable practice, which tends to produce more robust and flexible learning than repeating one thing in isolation (Shea & Morgan, 1979; see Chapter 7).

The brain that learned to juggle

In January 2004, a short paper in Nature changed how scientists thought about the adult brain. Bogdan Draganski, Arne May, and colleagues recruited 24 young adults (mean age 22) with no juggling experience and divided them into two groups. One group was given three months to learn the three-ball cascade. When they could sustain it for at least 60 seconds, their brains were scanned with MRI. They were scanned again three months later, after a period without practice.

The jugglers showed a significant, transient expansion of grey matter in two regions: the mid-temporal area known as hMT/V5, which processes visual motion, on both sides of the brain, and the left posterior intraparietal sulcus, involved in linking vision to action. Non-jugglers showed no such change. Three months after practice stopped, the expansion had decreased, and most jugglers could no longer juggle fluently (Draganski et al., 2004).

This was among the first clear demonstrations that learning a new skill could produce a structural change, visible on an MRI scan, in the healthy adult human brain. Later studies extended it:

  • The changes can appear within seven days of starting to learn, and seem to depend on learning something new more than on continued exercise of an already-learned skill (Driemeyer et al., 2008).
  • Older adults (around 60) can learn the cascade too, though less proficiently than young adults, and show similar grey-matter changes in hMT/V5, plus transient increases in the left hippocampus and in the nucleus accumbens (Boyke et al., 2008).
  • White matter changes too. After six weeks of juggling practice, Scholz and colleagues (2009) found increased fractional anisotropy, a measure of white-matter microstructure, beneath the right posterior intraparietal sulcus, and this was still evident four weeks after training ended.
  • Expert jugglers, who could juggle at least five balls, had higher grey-matter density than non-jugglers in visual-motion and intraparietal regions, and within the experts, performance correlated with grey-matter density in right hMT+/V5 (Gerber et al., 2014).

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established, with caveats. Learning to juggle ordinary balls is associated with measurable, region-specific, and partly transient changes in adult brain structure, in young and older adults (Draganski et al., 2004; Driemeyer et al., 2008; Boyke et al., 2008; Scholz et al., 2009). The changes are mainly in regions for seeing motion and linking vision to action, not in “fighting” or general-intelligence regions. Chapter 6 discusses the important methodological debates about such findings.

Now make them iron

Here is where honesty matters most.

Every one of those brain studies used ordinary juggling balls. Typical juggling balls weigh on the order of a hundred-odd grams. A six-pound iron ball weighs about 2.7 kilograms, roughly twenty times as much. Three of them together weigh more than eight kilograms. No published study has examined the brain, the body, or the injury risk of juggling balls this heavy.

That does not mean heavy juggling has no effects. It almost certainly has large ones. But they are not the same effects, and they cannot be borrowed from the light-ball studies. Consider what changes when the ball gets twenty times heavier:

  • The physics of the catch. Kinetic energy scales with mass. A ball falling about half a metre arrives with roughly twenty times the energy if it is twenty times heavier. For a 2.7 kg ball dropped from 0.5 m, that is about 13 joules, compared with well under one joule for a light juggling ball. The hand, wrist, elbow, and shoulder must absorb that energy on every catch, over and over.
  • The pattern. Heavy balls cannot be thrown as high or as fast. The pattern becomes lower and tighter, more like a series of cradled catches and drives than airy throws. The timing relationships that Beek and Turvey studied will be different.
  • The demand. Light juggling is overwhelmingly a visuomotor skill. Heavy juggling is also a strength-endurance task, an eccentric (lengthening) loading task for the forearms and shoulders, and a test of grip.
  • The risk. A dropped juggling bag is a joke. A dropped six-pound iron ball is a broken toe, a damaged floor, or, if it is mis-thrown toward the face, a serious injury.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Plausible but untested. It is reasonable to expect heavy-ball juggling to train grip endurance, eccentric control of the forearms and shoulders, and trunk stability, because those tissues are clearly loaded. It is also reasonable to expect it to retain some of juggling’s visuomotor and attentional demands. But there are no studies of heavy-ball juggling. The size, nature, and safety of its effects are unknown.

Regenerative power

The System’s central claim for the iron balls is continuous regenerative power: the ball is absorbed on the catch and its momentum is reversed into the next throw, so that force is recycled rather than wasted.

As physics, this is a real and elegant idea. Muscles and tendons act partly like springs. In many movements, from running to jumping, the body stores elastic energy when a muscle-tendon unit is stretched under load and releases some of it in the following shortening, a pattern sports scientists call the stretch-shortening cycle. A heavy ball caught with a yielding hand and immediately redirected upward fits that pattern well. A juggler who learns to “give” with the catch and turn the give into the throw is learning to use the elastic and reflexive properties of the arm, rather than fighting the ball with stiff muscle.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Practitioner claim. That this regenerative pattern transfers to striking (“chamber-to-impact without energy leakage”), blocking (“receive and redirect force”), clinch, trapping, and awareness of multiple threats is the system’s claim. It has not been measured. There are no studies of heavy juggling and fighting outcomes, and no recorded bouts or force data. See below for why such transfer cannot be assumed.

Tracking many things at once

One of the claimed benefits of juggling is predictive tracking of multiple objects. There is a real science of this. Since the 1980s, psychologists have studied “multiple object tracking”: people’s ability to follow several moving targets at once among distractors. Pylyshyn and Storm (1988) showed that people can track several independently moving targets in parallel. And research on expert athletes shows that experts are better at picking up perceptual cues and anticipating what will happen next, using fewer, longer visual fixations than novices (Mann et al., 2007).

Juggling clearly exercises a version of this capacity: three objects, predicted, intercepted, and released in rhythm. But there is a crucial gap between “juggling trains the ability to track juggling balls” and “juggling trains the ability to track opponents.” That gap is the problem of transfer.

The problem of transfer

Generations of educators hoped that training one skill would improve many others, that Latin would sharpen the mind, that chess would make children smarter. Modern research has been sobering. Meta-analyses of chess, music, and working-memory training find that apparent “far transfer” to unrelated abilities mostly disappears in well-designed studies with active control groups (Sala & Gobet, 2017). A major review of commercial “brain training” found strong evidence that people get better at the trained tasks, weaker evidence for improvement on closely related tasks, and little evidence for improvement in everyday cognitive performance (Simons et al., 2016).

Motor skills follow a similar principle, often called specificity: we get best at what we actually practice. Juggling trains predictive visuomotor timing with objects on ballistic arcs. Dropping an opponent requires contact, structure, and timing under live, unpredictable resistance, which in practice means sparring and partner work.

That does not mean heavy juggling is useless for a fighter. It may well build tissue capacity, grip, endurance, rhythm, and composure that a fighter can use. But the honest statement is this: the transfer of juggling to fighting is a hypothesis, not a finding. If you care about fighting, you will need to train fighting, too, and the System, wisely, includes the heavy bag and dummy for exactly that reason.

We get best at what we actually practice. Everything else is a hypothesis worth testing.

What the iron balls offer

Set the unmeasured claims aside, and a great deal remains.

The cascade, Mills Mess, and Box are among the richest coordination patterns a human being can learn. Learning them, even with ordinary balls, is associated with measurable changes in the adult brain. Juggling demands, and rewards, a quality of attention that is total but relaxed, focused on the whole pattern rather than any single ball. And, once a body has been properly prepared over a long time, heavier balls add a strength-endurance and grip dimension that the light-ball studies never touched.

The path in, as Chapter 12 describes, begins exactly where the science begins: with light balls, and a single minute of cascade.

The Spinning Ring Iron Bar

Chapter 4

A ring that will not stay centered unless you do.

The second tool of the System of Inevitability is, as far as this book can determine, unique. There are maces, clubs, staffs, and barbells in every strength tradition on earth. But a five-foot stainless-steel bar weighing 25 pounds, held palms-down, with a 6-inch, 2-pound iron ring kept spinning around it, centered, in both directions, while the body walks and turns, is something else.

What the bar asks

Think about what is required to keep that ring spinning in the middle of the bar.

The ring does not spin by itself. It must be driven by small, rhythmic, circular movements of the bar: a continuous wobble transmitted from the hands through the steel. Too little drive and the ring slows and drops. Too much in one direction and it drifts toward one hand. Any tilt of the bar sends it sliding. So the practitioner must, all at once:

  • hold a long, heavy lever steady against gravity, with the weight spread across a wide grip;
  • produce a continuous, small-amplitude circular motion in the wrists, forearms, and shoulders;
  • sense, mostly by feel, where the ring is and how fast it is spinning;
  • correct the bar’s tilt and drive continuously to keep the ring centered;
  • reverse the direction of spin at will;
  • and do all of this overhead, at an angle with the back arched, or pushed out from the chest, sometimes while walking and turning.

That is a remarkable combination. It is a strength-endurance task for the grip, forearms, and shoulders; an instability task, because the load is always shifting; and a perceptual task, because success depends on reading subtle feedback through the hands.

The family resemblance: maces and clubs

The bar’s closest relatives with any scientific literature are the steel mace (a long handle with a weighted head, swung in circles and arcs) and the Indian club (a bottle-shaped club swung in loops around the body). Both come from long traditions of wrestling and martial conditioning in South and West Asia, and both have seen a modern revival.

Until recently, there was almost no controlled research on them. That has started to change.

The 2026 mace trial

In January 2026, BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation published a randomized controlled trial by Akaras and colleagues on mace training in elite wrestlers. This is the trial referenced in the System of Inevitability’s viability assessment, and its details were verified for this book.

Thirty national- and international-level male wrestlers (aged 18 to 30) were randomized; 27 completed the study. Thirteen added mace training to their normal wrestling programme three times a week for twelve weeks; fourteen continued their normal programme. Each mace session lasted about 15 minutes, with the mace set at 20% of body weight. The programme progressed from basic two-handed swings to single-arm, multi-planar, and “360” swings over the twelve weeks.

Compared with the control group, the mace group improved significantly more in:

  • grip strength in both the dominant and non-dominant hands;
  • shoulder flexibility (on the dominant side, for external rotation);
  • shoulder internal and external rotator strength;
  • closed-kinetic-chain upper-extremity stability (the CKCUEST, a test we will use in Chapter 12);
  • push-up endurance.

One outcome did not improve: shoulder proprioception, measured as the ability to reproduce joint angles of 60 and 120 degrees without vision. The authors suggested that mace work emphasizes dynamic, global stability rather than the precise, angle-specific sense of position that this test measures (Akaras et al., 2026).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Suggestive. One randomized trial in 27 elite male wrestlers found that 12 weeks of added mace training improved grip strength, shoulder rotator strength, shoulder flexibility, CKCUEST stability, and push-up endurance, but not shoulder joint-position sense (Akaras et al., 2026). The authors themselves note a small sample, a single training environment, no follow-up, and no measures of match performance or injury.

There is one more detail worth knowing. According to the published methods, the mace group followed a progressive programme, while the control group’s training volume and intensity stayed constant for twelve weeks. That means part of the mace group’s advantage may come simply from having a progressive, extra training stimulus, rather than from the mace as such. This does not make the trial worthless. It makes it a promising first step, not a final word.

Indian clubs and clubbells

Two small randomized studies by Walter and colleagues have examined light club training for the shoulder. In female handball players, an eight-week clubbell programme (three days a week, twenty minutes a day, with clubs of only 0.5 kg and then 1 kg) improved dominant-arm internal-rotator strength compared with handball training alone, and within the club group, internal-rotation range of motion and rotator strength improved (Walter et al., 2023). A similar study examined cricket fast bowlers’ shoulder kinematics after Indian-clubbell exercise (Walter, Moltchanova, & Petersen, 2023).

Notice the loads: half a kilogram to one kilogram. These are light tools, used carefully and progressively, and they produced measurable changes in shoulder strength and mobility. That is a useful lesson for anyone tempted to start heavy.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Suggestive. Small randomized studies suggest that light club training (0.5–1 kg) can improve shoulder rotator strength and range of motion in throwing athletes (Walter et al., 2023; Walter, Moltchanova, & Petersen, 2023). The samples are small and the populations specific.

What the mace and club studies do not tell us

It is tempting to say: maces improve grip and shoulder stability, so the spinning ring bar must too. That inference is understandable, and possibly even correct, but it is not evidence. The differences are large:

  • A mace concentrates its weight at one end of a lever and is swung. The ring bar spreads 25 pounds across a five-foot bar held in two hands, and the ring is spun on it.
  • The mace trial used a load of 20% of body weight, swung in large arcs. The ring bar involves small, continuous oscillations to drive the ring, plus static holding of a long lever.
  • The bar’s unique element, a freely moving ring that must be kept centered, introduces a perceptual-control demand that has no analogue in the mace studies.
  • The bar is also worked at about 45 degrees with a back-bend, a position that loads the lumbar spine in extension. No study of maces or clubs addresses that.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Practitioner claims. The System of Inevitability claims that the spinning ring bar builds grip, forearm, and wrist resilience; rotator cuff and scapular stability; rotational core power; proprioceptive acuity; and tendon durability under persistent multi-planar instability. Several of these are plausible given what the bar demands and given related research on maces, clubs, instability, and tendon loading. None has been measured for this implement. Interestingly, the one trial on a related implement found no improvement in a standard proprioception test, which is a reason for caution about the proprioceptive-acuity claim specifically.

Instability and the shoulder

Why might an unstable load be valuable at all? The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, and that mobility is paid for with reduced passive stability. The rotator cuff and the muscles that control the shoulder blade (scapula) must constantly fine-tune the position of the joint. Movements that require continuous small corrections, as the ring bar does, plausibly exercise exactly that control.

Research on proprioceptive and neuromuscular training supports the general principle. Systematic reviews find that training programmes designed to challenge balance and joint control reduce some sports injuries, particularly ankle sprains and knee injuries in pivoting sports (Hübscher et al., 2010), and that proprioceptive training can improve sensorimotor function (Aman et al., 2015). But, as Chapter 8 explains, those findings come mostly from lower-limb programmes in young athletes, and they do not automatically apply to a heavy overhead implement.

The back-bend

The System describes working the bar “at 45 degrees with back-bend.” This deserves a plain warning.

⚠ Caution

Caution: overhead load in spinal extension. Holding a 25 lb lever overhead or at an angle while arching the lower back combines two demanding things: a long, heavy lever on the shoulders, and extension load on the lumbar spine. Done by an adapted practitioner with control, it may be an excellent challenge. Attempted by a beginner, or when fatigued, it is a recipe for low-back strain or shoulder injury. Begin with a broomstick or a light dowel, without a back-bend, and add extension only gradually and only if it is pain-free. See Chapter 12.

What the bar offers

Strip away the claims and the bar remains a brilliant piece of design. It turns strength into a conversation. The ring is a feedback device, an honest and immediate reporter of whether your hands, wrists, shoulders, and trunk are organized. It cannot be fooled by effort. It responds only to control.

That property, immediate, unambiguous feedback about a continuous action, is one of the classic preconditions for skill learning (Wolpert et al., 2011) and for flow (see Chapter 9). It may be the most important thing about the bar. You cannot spin the ring centered while thinking about something else.

The ring cannot be fooled by effort. It responds only to control.

The path in is gentle: a broomstick, a light ring or even a loose hoop of rope, short sets, no back-bend, and patience. The bar, like the iron balls, is a destination, not a starting point.

Bag, Dummy, and Stone

Chapter 5

Sooner or later, force has to meet something.

The iron balls and the ring bar train the body to produce and recycle force in the air. But a fighter, a mason, or anyone who works with the physical world must also learn what happens when force meets resistance. That is the role of the System’s “overlay” tools: the heavy bag, the metal-armed dummy, and, beneath both, the long apprenticeship of stone.

The heavy bag

A heavy bag is, in a sense, the simplest piece of honest equipment in martial arts. It pushes back. Strike it with poor alignment and the wrist folds, the elbow jars, or the shoulder feels the shock. Strike it well and force travels cleanly from the ground through the legs, hips, trunk, and arm into the bag.

That is exactly the kind of feedback a solitary practitioner needs. The bag cannot coach you, but it reports every structural mistake in the language of discomfort. Over time, a practitioner learns to align the body so that impact is absorbed by structure rather than by small joints.

The metal-armed dummy

The wooden dummy (in Cantonese, muk yan jong) is a classic training tool of Wing Chun: a post with protruding arms and a leg, against which a practitioner rehearses blocks, traps, and strikes in continuous flowing sequences. The System of Inevitability uses a custom version with arms made of schedule-40 steel pipe.

A dummy trains something the bag does not: contact geometry. Its arms occupy fixed angles in space. Working around them, a practitioner learns to receive, deflect, and redirect, to move the body around a fixed structure, and to keep the arms in alignment while turning and stepping. Metal arms are less forgiving than wood. They teach precision through consequence.

What the research says about hard martial arts

There is a modest research literature on the health effects of martial arts. A systematic review of 28 studies of “hard” martial arts (those that use body-contact techniques) in adults found that most reported benefits for balance, cognitive function, and psychological health, and that benefits appeared regardless of the age at which people began. The reviewers also cautioned that the quality of evidence is limited by methodological weaknesses across the studies (Origua Rios et al., 2018).

Related traditions with slower, more meditative movement have been studied more extensively. A meta-analysis of tai chi in older adults found improvements in executive function and global cognition, while calling for larger and more rigorous trials (Wayne et al., 2014).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Suggestive. Martial arts practice is associated with improvements in balance, cognition, and psychological health in adults, but the studies are of variable quality (Origua Rios et al., 2018). No study has examined bag-and-dummy training as practiced in the System of Inevitability.

The specificity of contact skill

Here we return to the most important lesson in Chapter 3. In motor learning, we get best at what we actually practice. The bag and dummy are valuable precisely because they bring the System closer to the real task of contact. They supply something juggling and the ring bar cannot: force meeting resistance, structure under impact, timing against an object.

But even the bag and dummy are not opponents. They do not move unpredictably, they do not hit back, and they do not try to deceive you. In every combat tradition that has been tested against resistance, skill in actually using technique against a person requires training with people: partner drills, pressure testing, and sparring. Expertise in sport depends heavily on reading an opponent’s movement and anticipating their actions (Mann et al., 2007), and that perceptual skill is built in the presence of real opponents.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Practitioner claim, untested. The System’s statement that its tools build “opponent-dropping” capacity is the practitioner’s claim. There are no recorded bouts, force measurements, or independent practitioners who have been tested. Anyone whose goal is self-defense or combat should combine conditioning practices like these with qualified, supervised partner training.

Stone: the occupational base

Beneath all of this lies something easy to overlook: twenty-five years of stonemasonry.

Occupational loading is training. A mason lifts, carries, rotates, and places heavy, irregular objects for hours a day, year after year. That is a vast accumulated dose of grip work, forearm loading, trunk stabilization, and carrying. As Chapter 8 explains, tendons and other connective tissues adapt to loading slowly, over months and years, and the ability to tolerate high loads is built gradually through exactly this kind of long, consistent exposure (Bohm et al., 2015; Magnusson & Kjaer, 2019).

This has a direct, practical implication. The loads used in the System of Inevitability, 6 lb balls and a 25 lb bar, sit on top of a body prepared by decades of manual work. A beginner who copies the loads without copying the decades is skipping the foundation. That is not a criticism of the System. It is simply an honest reading of how bodies adapt.

A beginner who copies the loads without copying the decades is skipping the foundation.

Hands that are cared for

Bag work and dummy work load the hands, wrists, and forearms with repeated impacts. Juggling heavy balls loads them with repeated catches. Stonework loads them all day. Hands are precious. A few principles, drawn from general good practice rather than from any study specific to this System:

  • Build up impact gradually: light contact before hard contact, short rounds before long ones.
  • Protect the wrists: keep them aligned with the forearm on impact; consider hand wraps and gloves on the bag, especially early.
  • Respect pain in small joints. Joint pain that persists into the next day is a signal to reduce load, not to “push through.”
  • Rest. Tissues adapt between sessions, not during them.

Chapter 12 turns these principles into a structured, suggested progression.

What the contact tools offer

The bag and dummy are where the System’s air-borne geometry is asked to become structure. They are its reality check. And by including them, the System implicitly acknowledges something wise: that rhythm and spiral, however beautiful, must eventually meet resistance to become useful.

In that sense the overlay tools are not an afterthought. They are where the practice becomes honest with itself.

Part III · The Science

What changes in a brain that learns, a body that adapts, and a mind that pays attention?

The Brain That Learns

Chapter 6

Learning is not something that happens to the brain. It is something the brain becomes.

For much of the twentieth century, a common assumption held that the adult brain was essentially fixed. You could learn facts and habits, of course, but the physical structure of the brain was thought to be largely set after childhood, changing afterward mainly through ageing or disease. Learning was imagined as rearranging the furniture, not rebuilding the house.

That picture has changed profoundly, and juggling played a starring role in changing it.

Three months, three balls

We met the key study in Chapter 3. In 2004, Draganski and colleagues taught young adults the three-ball cascade over three months and scanned their brains before training, after they could juggle for at least 60 seconds, and three months after they stopped. The jugglers’ grey matter expanded transiently in hMT/V5, a region specialized for perceiving visual motion, and in the left posterior intraparietal sulcus, which helps link what we see to how we act. The expansion was related to juggling performance, absent in non-jugglers, and decreased once practice stopped (Draganski et al., 2004).

The authors drew a striking conclusion: juggling, and “consequently the perception and spatial anticipation of moving objects,” was a stronger stimulus for structural change in visual areas than in the motor areas one might expect. Learning to juggle, in other words, changes how the brain sees moving things.

What followed

Over the next decade, the juggling paradigm became a workhorse of plasticity research.

Fast. A follow-up with 20 adults found that grey matter in the occipito-temporal cortex could change after just seven days of juggling practice. Neither performance level alone nor amount of exercise alone explained the changes, leading the authors to suggest that “the qualitative change (i.e. learning of a new task) is more critical for the brain to change its structure than continued training of an already-learned task” (Driemeyer et al., 2008).

That is a profound and practical idea. The brain seems to respond most to novelty: to the challenge of learning something it cannot yet do.

At any age. The same group then studied healthy older adults, around 60 years old. They learned the cascade, though less proficiently than 20-year-olds, and showed similar grey-matter changes in hMT/V5. They also showed transient increases in the left hippocampus, a structure central to memory, and in the nucleus accumbens, involved in motivation and reward (Boyke et al., 2008).

A very large behavioural study supports the same message. Voelcker-Rehage and Willimczik (2006) taught a juggling task to 1,206 people aged 6 to 89 with no prior juggling experience. After instruction and six practice sessions, older adults improved clearly, reaching performance comparable to children aged 10 to 14 and adults aged 30 to 59. The authors concluded that older adults “exhibit high reserve capacity,” that is, “a potential for learning ‘new’ motor skills.”

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established. Older adults can learn new, complex motor skills like juggling, and show measurable training-related changes in brain structure, though typically less pronounced performance than young adults (Boyke et al., 2008; Voelcker-Rehage & Willimczik, 2006).

In the wiring. Grey matter is where neurons’ cell bodies and synapses concentrate. White matter is the brain’s wiring: bundles of nerve fibres, many wrapped in insulating myelin. After six weeks of juggling, Scholz and colleagues (2009) found increased fractional anisotropy, a diffusion-MRI measure of white-matter microstructure, in the white matter underlying the right posterior intraparietal sulcus, persisting four weeks after training ended. This was, as the authors put it, among the first evidence “for training-related changes in white-matter structure in the healthy human adult brain.” White-matter plasticity in adults has since become an active field in its own right (Sampaio-Baptista & Johansen-Berg, 2017).

In experts. Expert jugglers who could juggle at least five balls had higher grey-matter density than non-jugglers in visual-motion and intraparietal regions, and in the jugglers, the density in right hMT+/V5 correlated with performance (Gerber et al., 2014).

Who learns fastest. In a six-week juggling study, people with more grey matter in medial occipito-parietal regions at the start learned faster, and better performers showed larger grey-matter increases in parietal and motor cortex in the weeks after training (Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2014). Brains differ, and practice and performance both shape how much they change.

What is actually changing?

When an MRI scan shows “more grey matter,” what is physically different? The honest answer is that MRI cannot see individual cells, so we do not know for certain. Researchers have proposed several possibilities, based mostly on animal studies: growth of new synapses and dendritic spines, changes in supporting glial cells, growth of blood vessels, and, in white matter, changes in myelination and in the organization of axons (Zatorre et al., 2012). The likely truth is some combination, varying by region and timescale.

A necessary caution

Science advances partly by doubting its own exciting findings. In 2013, Thomas and Baker published a critical review of training-dependent structural plasticity in humans. They argued that limitations of experimental design, statistical methods, and imaging artefacts “may underlie many of the reported effects,” and that the most robust evidence then available was for changes in hippocampal volume with exercise in older adults, rather than in the neocortex (Thomas & Baker, 2013).

That critique does not erase the juggling findings. Several of them have been repeated in different samples, and they fit with animal research. But it is an important reminder that MRI measures of brain structure are indirect, that effects in small studies can be overestimated, and that the step from “a region looks slightly different on a scan” to “this person has become better at something important” is long.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Where the debate lies. That adult brains change functionally with learning is beyond doubt. That they change structurally in ways visible on MRI is supported by multiple studies, including several with juggling, but the size, reliability, and cellular meaning of these changes are still debated (Thomas & Baker, 2013; Zatorre et al., 2012).

Exercise and the brain

Juggling is not the only path to a changing brain. Physical exercise itself has some of the best evidence in the field.

In a randomized controlled trial with 120 older adults, a year of aerobic exercise training increased the size of the anterior hippocampus by about 2%, “effectively reversing age-related loss in volume by 1 to 2 years,” and improved spatial memory. The control group’s hippocampal volume declined (Erickson et al., 2011). This is the finding Thomas and Baker identified as among the most robust.

How might exercise do this? One candidate messenger is brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein that supports the survival and growth of neurons. A meta-analysis of 29 studies found that a single session of exercise produced a moderate increase in BDNF levels, that regular exercise intensified that effect, and that regular exercise produced a small increase in resting BDNF (Szuhany et al., 2015).

And the cognitive benefits are not limited to the young. A meta-analysis of 36 randomized trials in adults over 50 found that physical exercise improved cognitive function, with aerobic exercise, resistance training, multicomponent training, and tai chi all showing benefits; sessions of 45 to 60 minutes at least at moderate intensity were associated with better results (Northey et al., 2018).

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established. Regular physical exercise improves cognitive function in adults over 50 (Northey et al., 2018), and aerobic training can increase hippocampal volume and memory in older adults (Erickson et al., 2011). Exercise raises BDNF, a plausible contributor (Szuhany et al., 2015).

The System of Inevitability is not primarily aerobic. But heavy juggling and continuous bar work, sustained for many minutes, are physically demanding whole-body activities. They plausibly combine two of the brain’s favourite stimuli: novel skill learning and physical effort. That combination is attractive, though, again, it has not been studied directly.

Sleep: where practice becomes skill

There is one more ingredient in the plastic brain, and it happens when you are not training at all.

In a well-known study, Walker and colleagues (2002) found that a night of sleep after practicing a motor sequence produced about a 20% increase in speed without a loss of accuracy, while an equivalent period awake produced no significant benefit. The improvement correlated with the amount of a particular stage of sleep (stage 2 non-REM), especially late in the night.

The practical meaning is simple and lovely: practice, then sleep. Some of the learning you start in the evening is finished while you dream.

Spacing: the patience of plasticity

If novelty triggers change and sleep consolidates it, how should practice be distributed? Motor-learning research consistently favours spreading practice out. In one study, spacing practice sessions across days produced better learning of a motor skill than massing the same practice into one session (Shea et al., 2000).

This, too, has a direct practical implication. Twenty minutes a day for a week is generally better for learning than two hours on Sunday.

Use it, or it recedes

The most sobering juggling finding is also the most motivating. In Draganski’s study, the grey-matter expansion receded after three months without practice, and most participants could no longer juggle fluently. The brain invests in what you use, and withdraws investment from what you abandon.

That is not a reason for despair. It is a reason for practice: steady, lifelong, and renewed with fresh challenges. The brain, it seems, is less a monument than a garden.

The brain is less a monument than a garden. It invests in what you use.

What this means for a practitioner

Let us gather the threads into a few honest principles.

  1. Learning new things changes the brain. The strongest stimulus appears to be learning something you cannot yet do, not repeating what you already can (Driemeyer et al., 2008). Each new pattern, from Cascade to Mills Mess to Box, is a fresh invitation.
  2. It works at any age. Older adults learn new motor skills and show brain changes, though perhaps more slowly (Boyke et al., 2008; Voelcker-Rehage & Willimczik, 2006).
  3. Exercise helps the brain in its own right (Erickson et al., 2011; Northey et al., 2018).
  4. Sleep and spacing matter. Short, frequent sessions with good sleep beat marathon sessions (Walker et al., 2002; Shea et al., 2000).
  5. Changes are specific and can recede. Juggling changes regions for seeing and acting on motion. Those changes fade without practice. Nothing here shows that juggling builds general intelligence or fighting skill.

None of this requires six-pound iron balls. Every one of these findings was made with ordinary juggling balls, ordinary walking, ordinary sleep. The door to a changing brain is open to everyone.

How Skill Is Built

Chapter 7

The body is a prediction machine that learns from its mistakes.

Why does a juggler’s tenth attempt go better than the first, and the thousandth better than the tenth? The science of motor learning has spent more than a century on that question. Its answers are practical, sometimes surprising, and directly useful to anyone practicing alone.

The predicting body

Every skilled movement depends on prediction. When you throw a ball, your nervous system does not wait to see where it lands before preparing the catch. It predicts the ball’s path, sends commands to the catching hand in advance, and then compares what actually happens with what it expected.

In a widely cited review, Wolpert, Diedrichsen, and Flanagan (2011) described several principles that seem to govern how the brain learns movement. Among them:

  • Error-based learning. The nervous system uses the difference between predicted and actual outcomes, the “prediction error,” to update its internal models of the body and the world. Each slightly mis-thrown ball teaches.
  • Reinforcement. Successful outcomes strengthen the movements that produced them.
  • Use-dependent learning. Simply repeating a movement biases future movements toward it.
  • Optimal control. Skilled performers do not control every detail rigidly. They control what matters for the goal and let the rest vary.

That last principle is beautifully visible in juggling. Experts do not throw each ball identically. They allow natural variability and correct only what threatens the pattern. It is also, perhaps, what the System of Inevitability means by continuous motion: not a fixed form repeated, but a living pattern sustained.

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established. Motor learning involves predictive internal models updated by error, reinforcement of successful actions, and use-dependent changes; skilled control focuses on task-relevant variables (Wolpert et al., 2011).

Variety beats repetition, in the long run

Here is one of the most counter-intuitive findings in the field. In 1979, Shea and Morgan had people learn three different movement patterns. One group practiced them in blocks: all of pattern A, then all of B, then all of C. Another group practiced them in a random, interleaved order. During practice, the blocked group performed better. But on later tests of retention and transfer, the random group did better. This became known as the contextual interference effect (Shea & Morgan, 1979).

The likely reason is that switching between tasks forces the brain to retrieve and rebuild each movement plan fresh, which is harder in the moment but builds more durable learning.

For a practitioner, the lesson is to mix it up once the basics are in place. Alternating Cascade, Mills Mess, and Box within a session, rather than drilling one for an hour, may feel clumsier, and is likely to produce more robust skill.

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established, with nuance. Interleaved (random) practice of several related skills often impairs performance during practice but improves later retention and transfer, compared with blocked practice (Shea & Morgan, 1979). The effect is strongest once learners have basic competence; complete beginners may benefit from some blocked practice first.

Where you put your attention

What should you think about while practicing? Gabriele Wulf and colleagues have studied this for decades. A large body of experiments finds that directing attention to the effect of a movement on the environment, an external focus (for example, “the arc of the ball” or “the ring staying centered”), tends to produce better performance and learning than directing attention to the body’s own movements, an internal focus (for example, “my wrist” or “my elbow”) (Wulf, 2013).

This finding is remarkably well-suited to the System’s tools. The ring on the bar is a perfect external focus. You cannot keep it centered by thinking about your wrists. You keep it centered by attending to the ring.

Wulf and Lewthwaite later combined this with two motivational factors in the OPTIMAL theory of motor learning (“Optimizing Performance Through Intrinsic Motivation and Attention for Learning”). The theory proposes that learning is enhanced by an external focus, by enhanced expectancies (confidence that one can succeed), and by autonomy (some choice and control over one’s practice) (Wulf & Lewthwaite, 2016).

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established (external focus); influential theory (OPTIMAL). An external focus of attention generally improves motor performance and learning compared with an internal focus (Wulf, 2013). OPTIMAL theory adds confidence and autonomy as contributors (Wulf & Lewthwaite, 2016); its motivational components are more debated than the external-focus findings.

Choosing your own practice

The System of Inevitability is radically self-directed: no instructors, no syllabus. Is there any science on whether choosing your own practice helps?

There is, and it is more interesting than a simple yes.

Early experiments suggested that learners who could choose aspects of their own practice, for instance when to receive feedback, learned better than “yoked” learners who received the same practice schedule without choosing it (Chiviacowsky & Wulf, 2002). Later studies even found benefits from choices unrelated to the task itself, such as the colour of golf balls, suggesting a motivational effect of autonomy (Lewthwaite et al., 2015).

But in 2022, McKay and colleagues published a careful meta-analysis that corrected for publication bias, the tendency for positive results to be published and null results to be filed away. A naive analysis of 52 experiments found a moderate benefit of self-controlled practice. After correcting for selective reporting, the estimated effect shrank to a small one (g ≈ 0.11), and the authors concluded that “the benefit of self-controlled practice on motor learning is small and not currently distinguishable from zero” (McKay et al., 2022).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Contested. Choosing aspects of your own practice may help motor learning, possibly through motivation (Chiviacowsky & Wulf, 2002; Lewthwaite et al., 2015), but a bias-corrected meta-analysis found the average benefit to be small and uncertain (McKay et al., 2022).

What should a solitary practitioner take from that? Perhaps this: autonomy is not a magic accelerator of learning, but it may be crucial for something else, staying with practice at all. People persist with activities that feel like their own. We return to that, and to the broader evidence on autonomy and motivation, in Chapter 11.

How much does practice matter?

Popular culture loves the idea that ten thousand hours of practice makes an expert. It traces partly to a classic paper by Ericsson, Krampe, and Tesch-Römer (1993), which argued that expert performance reflects long periods of deliberate practice: effortful, focused activity designed specifically to improve, typically with feedback.

That paper transformed how people think about expertise. But a later meta-analysis put numbers to the idea and found that deliberate practice explained about 26% of the variance in performance for games, 21% for music, 18% for sports, 4% for education, and less than 1% for professions. The authors’ conclusion is a good one to keep: “deliberate practice is important, but not as important as has been argued” (Macnamara et al., 2014).

Other things also matter: when you started, your body, your genes, your teachers, your opportunities, your sleep, your luck. That is not discouraging. It simply means that practice is the part of the equation you control, and that comparing yourself with anyone else is pointless.

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established. Deliberate practice substantially contributes to skill in games, music, and sport, but explains well under half of individual differences in performance (Macnamara et al., 2014).

Expertise is mostly seeing

What separates experts from novices in sport? A meta-analysis of 42 studies found that experts are better at picking up perceptual cues, responding more accurately and more quickly, and that they use fewer visual fixations of longer duration, including longer “quiet eye” periods before acting (Mann et al., 2007).

Combine this with the juggling gaze study in Chapter 3, where experts tracked each ball less than intermediates did (Huys & Beek, 2002), and a picture emerges. With skill, perception becomes economical. The expert does not look harder. The expert looks less, and sees more, because prediction fills the gaps.

That is perhaps the most beautiful finding in this chapter, and the one closest to what contemplative traditions mean by soft eyes or a wide gaze: attention that rests on the whole rather than grasping at the parts.

The expert does not look harder. The expert looks less, and sees more.

The limits of transfer, revisited

If skill is built through specific practice, how far does it spread? Chapter 3 introduced the evidence: far transfer from one trained skill to unrelated abilities is rare in well-controlled studies (Sala & Gobet, 2017; Simons et al., 2016).

This does not mean that nothing transfers. General capacities, such as strength, endurance, tissue tolerance, and perhaps calm under pressure, can carry over to many activities. But specific skills, the fine-tuned predictions and timings that make a juggler a juggler or a fighter a fighter, are largely built by practicing them specifically.

For the System of Inevitability, the honest formulation is this. The tools almost certainly build general physical capacities that a martial artist can use. Whether they build martial skill is an open question that only testing against resistance can answer.

Practical principles for the solitary learner

From all of this, a handful of evidence-based principles follow. They are summarized here and built into the progression in Chapter 12.

  1. Make errors safely. Error drives learning, so practice at the edge of your ability, but with tools light enough that errors cost nothing.
  2. Focus outward. Attend to the ball’s arc or the ring’s centre, not your joints (Wulf, 2013).
  3. Mix it up once the basics are in place. Interleave patterns and tools (Shea & Morgan, 1979).
  4. Space your practice. Short sessions on many days (Shea et al., 2000).
  5. Sleep on it (Walker et al., 2002).
  6. Own your practice. Choose your path, because it keeps you practicing, even if it does not magically speed learning (McKay et al., 2022).
  7. Measure. Without measurement, self-directed practice cannot tell improvement from hope. Chapter 12 gives you three simple tests.
  8. Test transfer, don’t assume it. If you want a skill, practice that skill.

The Body That Adapts

Chapter 8

Tissues are not built in the session. They are built in the days after it.

The System of Inevitability talks about grip, tendons, rotator cuffs, proprioceptive acuity, and structural integrity. These are not abstractions. They are tissues and senses, each with its own biology, its own speed of adaptation, and its own way of breaking when pushed too fast. This chapter looks at what science knows about each.

The sixth sense: proprioception

Close your eyes and touch your nose. You can do it because of proprioception, your sense of the position, movement, and force of your own body. It relies on receptors in muscles (muscle spindles, which sense stretch), in tendons (Golgi tendon organs, which sense tension), in joints, and in the skin, together with the brain’s own record of the commands it has sent. A major review describes proprioception as a family of senses signalling “body shape, body position and movement, and muscle force” (Proske & Gandevia, 2012).

Proprioception is what lets a juggler catch without looking at the hand, and what lets a practitioner feel the ring drifting on the bar before seeing it. It is, quite literally, the body’s awareness of itself.

Can proprioception be trained?

A systematic review of 51 studies of proprioceptive training found an average improvement of about 52% across outcome measures, with joint-position and target-reaching training consistently improving joint position sense. The authors described “converging evidence that proprioceptive training can yield meaningful improvements in somatosensory and sensorimotor function,” while noting that much more work is needed (Aman et al., 2015).

There is a caveat close to home. In the mace trial described in Chapter 4, twelve weeks of mace training did not improve a standard test of shoulder joint position sense, even while it improved strength and stability (Akaras et al., 2026). Proprioception, it seems, may improve most when it is trained specifically, which is, once again, the principle of specificity.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Suggestive. Targeted proprioceptive training appears to improve sensorimotor function (Aman et al., 2015), but general strength or implement training does not necessarily improve standard proprioception tests (Akaras et al., 2026). Whether heavy juggling or the ring bar improves proprioception has not been tested.

Balance, injury, and falls

The practical payoff of training balance and body control is best documented in two areas.

Sports injury. A systematic review of high-quality trials found that multi-component neuromuscular training reduced lower-limb injuries, acute knee injuries, and ankle sprains in young athletes in pivoting sports, and that balance training alone significantly reduced ankle sprains (Hübscher et al., 2010). A broader meta-analysis of 25 randomized trials with over 26,000 participants found that strength training reduced sports injuries to less than one-third, proprioception training roughly halved them, and stretching had no clear benefit (Lauersen et al., 2014).

Falls in older people. A Cochrane review of 108 randomized trials with more than 23,000 participants found, with high-certainty evidence, that exercise reduces the rate of falls in community-dwelling older people by about 23%, with balance and functional exercises particularly effective (Sherrington et al., 2019).

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established. Exercise programmes that include balance and strength reduce falls in older people (Sherrington et al., 2019) and sports injuries in athletes (Lauersen et al., 2014; Hübscher et al., 2010). Strength training is among the most protective interventions.

These findings concern balance and strength programmes generally, not the System’s tools specifically. But they establish something important: the capacities the System aims at are worth having, and they are trainable.

The handshake that predicts the future
