Of all the measures of physical health ever studied, one of the simplest is also one of the most revealing: how hard you can squeeze.

In midlife. In the Honolulu Heart Program, grip strength was measured in 6,089 healthy Japanese-American men aged 45 to 68, starting in 1965. Twenty-five years later, men in the lowest third of grip strength had nearly three times the odds of very slow walking speed compared with men in the highest third, and more than twice the risk of self-care disability (Rantanen et al., 1999).

Across the world. The PURE study measured grip strength in 139,691 adults in 17 countries of varying income. Over a median of four years, every 5 kg lower grip strength was associated with a 16% higher risk of death from any cause, and grip strength was a stronger predictor of all-cause and cardiovascular death than systolic blood pressure (Leong et al., 2015).

In half a million people. In the UK Biobank, with 502,293 participants aged 40 to 69, each 5 kg lower grip strength was associated with a 20% higher hazard of death from any cause in women and 16% in men, and with higher risk from cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, and several cancers (Celis-Morales et al., 2018).

Strength in general. In 8,762 men followed for an average of nearly 19 years, higher muscular strength was associated with lower death rates from all causes and from cancer, even after accounting for cardiorespiratory fitness (Ruiz et al., 2008). And a meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies found that doing muscle-strengthening activities was associated with 10–17% lower risk of death from any cause, cardiovascular disease, total cancer, diabetes, and lung cancer, with the greatest risk reduction at around 30–60 minutes per week (Momma et al., 2022).

Grip strength has been described as “an indispensable biomarker for older adults” (Bohannon, 2019).

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established association. Lower grip strength and lower muscular strength are consistently associated with higher risk of disability, disease, and death across large populations (Rantanen et al., 1999; Leong et al., 2015; Celis-Morales et al., 2018; Ruiz et al., 2008; Momma et al., 2022).

An important subtlety

These are associations. Grip strength is probably a window onto overall muscle health, activity, nutrition, and the absence of illness, rather than a magical property of the hands. The PURE authors explicitly call for research “to test whether improvement in strength reduces mortality.” Squeezing a gripper every day will make your grip stronger. It is not proven that this alone will make you live longer.

What the evidence does support is broader: building and keeping muscular strength across the body, through regular resistance activity, is associated with a longer, healthier life, and resistance training has well-documented benefits of its own. A practice like the System’s, which loads the grip heavily as part of whole-body work, is aligned with that evidence, even if it has not been studied directly.

Grip strength is a window onto the whole body’s health. Build the whole body, and the window brightens.

Tendons: the slow learners

If muscles are quick students, tendons are slow, careful ones.

Tendons transmit force from muscle to bone. They are made mostly of collagen arranged in a densely organized extracellular matrix, with relatively few cells and a modest blood supply. They adapt to mechanical loading, becoming stiffer and sometimes thicker, but the biology of that adaptation is complex and comparatively slow (Kjaer, 2004; Magnusson & Kjaer, 2019).

How tendons respond to training. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 studies in healthy adults found that exercise interventions of at least eight weeks increased tendon stiffness (standardized mean difference 0.70), elastic modulus (0.69), and, to a smaller degree, cross-sectional area (0.24). Stiffness adaptation depended significantly on loading intensity, and effects tended to be larger with interventions lasting twelve weeks or more (Bohm et al., 2015).

How slowly the core renews. A remarkable study used the carbon-14 released by nuclear bomb tests in the 1950s and 1960s as a natural tracer. Analysing Achilles tendons from people born between 1945 and 1983, the researchers found that the tendon core retained carbon-14 levels reflecting the first ~17 years of life, indicating that the core of the tendon “is formed during height growth and is essentially not renewed thereafter,” in contrast to muscle, which turns over continuously (Heinemeier et al., 2013). Adaptation in adulthood still occurs, but likely more at the tendon’s periphery and in its mechanical properties than through wholesale replacement.

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established. Tendons adapt to progressive, sufficiently intense loading over months, becoming stiffer (Bohm et al., 2015), but their biology is slow, and the adult tendon core turns over very little (Heinemeier et al., 2013; Magnusson & Kjaer, 2019).

Why this matters so much here

Muscles get stronger in weeks. Tendons take months to years to catch up. That mismatch is a classic setup for injury: an enthusiastic beginner builds enough muscle strength to move a heavy load before the tendons, and the small structures of the wrist, elbow, and shoulder, are ready to absorb it repeatedly.

The System of Inevitability’s claim of “tendon durability under persistent multiplanar instability” is plausible for a practitioner who has accumulated decades of gradual loading through stonemasonry and training. It is precisely what a beginner does not have. This is the single most important biological reason why the suggested progression in Chapter 12 begins with light tools and moves slowly.

Load, pain, and tendons

Tendon research also offers a hopeful note about pain. In a small, randomized crossover study of six volleyball players with patellar tendinopathy, a single session of isometric (static, holding) contractions reduced tendon pain immediately and for at least 45 minutes, more than isotonic contractions did (Rio et al., 2015). This is a small study and should not be over-applied, but it reflects a broader shift in sports medicine: well-dosed loading is often part of tendon treatment, not only a cause of tendon problems. If you have tendon pain, a physiotherapist can guide you.

The training-injury paradox

If load can injure, should we avoid it? The evidence says the opposite. In a widely cited review, Gabbett (2016) described a “training-injury prevention paradox”: athletes accustomed to high training loads often have fewer injuries than those training at lower workloads. The danger lies not in high load itself but in excessive and rapid increases in load. Gabbett argued that a large proportion of non-contact soft-tissue injuries are likely caused by such spikes.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Well-supported principle, debated details. Rapid spikes in training load are a common contributor to soft-tissue injury, while gradually accumulated high capacity is protective (Gabbett, 2016). The specific metrics used to monitor load (such as acute-to-chronic workload ratios) are debated; the core principle of gradual progression is not.

This is the paradox at the heart of the System of Inevitability. A body that has been gradually prepared for decades may thrive under loads that would injure a beginner. The loads are not the problem. The jump to the loads is.

The adapting body, summarized

  1. Proprioception is the body’s awareness of itself. It is trainable, especially with specific practice, but general strength training does not guarantee improvement on standard tests.
  2. Balance and strength training reduce falls in older adults and injuries in athletes. These are among the best-supported findings in exercise science.
  3. Grip and muscular strength are powerful markers of long-term health. Building whole-body strength is wise; grip alone is not a guarantee.
  4. Tendons adapt slowly, over months to years. Muscles outpace them, which is why beginners get hurt.
  5. Gradual progression is protective. Spikes in load are dangerous.

The body is listening to everything you do. It adapts to what you ask of it, if you ask patiently.

Attention, Flow, and Awareness

Chapter 9

You cannot spin the ring centered while thinking about something else.

We now arrive at the part of this book closest to its deepest hope: that practice can change not only what a body can do, but how a person experiences being alive. This is the territory of attention, flow, and awareness. It is also the territory where enthusiasm most easily outruns evidence. We will go carefully, and the view is worth it.

The wandering mind

In 2010, Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert used a smartphone app to ask thousands of people, at random moments throughout their days, what they were doing, what they were thinking about, and how they felt. Their finding was summarized in the title of their paper: A wandering mind is an unhappy mind. People were “thinking about what is not happening almost as often as they are thinking about what is,” and doing so “typically makes them unhappy” (Killingsworth & Gilbert, 2010).

This is one of the most quietly radical findings in modern psychology. It suggests that a great deal of everyday unhappiness comes not from our circumstances but from our absence from them: ruminating on the past, rehearsing the future, narrating ourselves to ourselves.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Robust finding, with interpretive caution. Mind-wandering is common and is associated, in experience-sampling data, with lower momentary happiness (Killingsworth & Gilbert, 2010). The association is clear; the direction of causation in daily life is more complex, since unhappiness can also cause mind-wandering.

Now consider three iron balls in the air. Or a ring spinning on a bar that will slide off the moment your attention drifts. These are activities that do not permit mind-wandering. They demand presence the way water demands that you swim.

Flow

The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi spent decades interviewing climbers, surgeons, chess players, dancers, and factory workers about the moments when they felt most fully alive. Again and again they described a similar state: complete absorption in a challenging activity, a merging of action and awareness, a loss of self-consciousness, a distorted sense of time, and a feeling that the activity was rewarding in itself. He called it flow (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990).

Flow is most likely when three conditions meet:

  1. Challenge matched to skill. Too easy, and we are bored. Too hard, and we are anxious. Flow lives in the narrow channel between.
  2. Clear goals. We know what we are trying to do, moment to moment.
  3. Immediate feedback. We know, instantly, how well we are doing.

Juggling and the ring bar satisfy these conditions almost perfectly. The goal is clear: keep the pattern going, keep the ring centered. Feedback is instant: the ball is caught or dropped; the ring holds or drifts. And the challenge can be adjusted endlessly: more balls, new patterns, heavier tools, walking while juggling, turning while spinning.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

The practice in practitioners’ words. The System of Inevitability’s emphasis on continuous motion, spirals “revealed in practice,” and movement in which each action flows from the last, reads very much like a description of flow from the inside. This is the practitioner’s experience and philosophy, not a measured outcome, but it fits the psychological description closely.

What happens in the brain during flow?

Flow has been studied in the laboratory. In one brain-imaging study, 27 participants solved mental arithmetic problems under three conditions: too easy (boredom), too hard (overload), and continuously adjusted to their skill (flow). The flow condition was associated with increased activity in parts of the left inferior frontal gyrus and putamen, and decreased activity in the medial prefrontal cortex and the amygdala. The authors interpreted these as reflecting a deeper sense of control, decreased self-referential processing, and decreased negative arousal (Ulrich et al., 2014).

That interpretation is striking. The medial prefrontal cortex is part of a network associated with thinking about oneself, the inner narrator. The amygdala is involved in threat and anxiety. In flow, both quieted.

An influential hypothesis, proposed by Arne Dietrich, suggested that flow involves “transient hypofrontality,” a temporary down-regulation of the brain’s explicit, analytical systems, allowing well-practiced implicit skills to run without interference (Dietrich, 2004). Later reviewers have found the neuroimaging evidence for hypofrontality “equivocal,” and have proposed instead that flow is best understood in terms of attention: efficient, absorbed engagement of higher-order attentional networks, with reduced activity in regions linked to self-referential processing (Harris, Vine, & Wilson, 2017).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Emerging. Neuroimaging studies associate flow with reduced activity in brain regions linked to self-referential thought and negative arousal (Ulrich et al., 2014; Harris, Vine, & Wilson, 2017). The “transient hypofrontality” hypothesis (Dietrich, 2004) remains a hypothesis, with mixed evidence.

Does flow make us perform better?

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 studies in sport and computer gaming found a medium-sized relationship between flow and performance (r = 0.31). But the authors stressed that the evidence “is unable to determine the causal direction” (Harris et al., 2023). Flow may improve performance; good performance may produce flow; probably both.

Either way, flow is worth cultivating for its own sake. People describe it as among the most rewarding experiences of their lives.

In flow, the inner narrator falls quiet, and the activity itself becomes the reward.

Mindfulness and moving meditation

Mindfulness, broadly, is the practice of attending to present-moment experience with openness rather than judgment. It has been studied extensively, and its evidence base is both genuinely positive and frequently overstated.

A rigorous systematic review and meta-analysis examined 47 randomized trials with active controls, totalling 3,515 participants. It found moderate evidence that mindfulness meditation programmes improved anxiety, depression, and pain, with effect sizes in the small-to-moderate range (for example, about 0.38 for anxiety and 0.30 for depression at eight weeks) (Goyal et al., 2014). A major neuroscience review describes mindfulness as involving at least three interacting components: enhanced attention control, improved emotion regulation, and altered self-awareness (Tang, Hölzel, & Posner, 2015).

At the same time, a group of fifteen researchers published a paper titled Mind the Hype, warning that “misinformation and poor methodology” in mindfulness research could leave the public “harmed, misled, and disappointed,” and calling for clearer definitions and better studies (Van Dam et al., 2018).

● Evidence: well-established

Moderately established. Mindfulness meditation programmes produce small-to-moderate improvements in anxiety, depression, and pain (Goyal et al., 2014). Claims beyond this, especially about dramatic brain or life transformations, are often overstated (Van Dam et al., 2018).

Is heavy juggling a form of mindfulness? Not by definition. Mindfulness practices usually cultivate open, non-judging awareness, while juggling demands narrowly focused task attention. But there is a family resemblance, and traditions of moving meditation, such as tai chi and qigong, sit somewhere between the two. As we saw in Chapter 5, tai chi has been associated with improved executive function in older adults (Wayne et al., 2014), and in a large network meta-analysis of exercise for depression, tai chi and qigong, yoga, walking, and strength training all reduced depressive symptoms (Noetel et al., 2024).

The honest claim is this: rhythmic, absorbing, whole-body practices share some features with meditation, especially present-moment attention and reduced self-narration, and some of them have been shown to benefit mood and cognition. Whether the System’s specific tools do so is untested.

Feeling from the inside: interoception

If proprioception is the sense of the body’s position, interoception is the sense of the body’s internal state: heartbeat, breath, hunger, temperature, tension, the visceral feel of emotion. Neuroscientist A. D. (Bud) Craig proposed that the anterior insula, a region deep in the brain, integrates these signals into a moment-by-moment representation of “how you feel,” and that this may be fundamental to human awareness itself (Craig, 2009).

Interoception is now a major research field. A consensus roadmap from leading researchers describes interoception as providing “a moment-by-moment mapping of the body’s internal landscape across conscious and unconscious levels,” and notes that disturbances of interoception are increasingly recognized in anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and addiction (Khalsa et al., 2018). Importantly, researchers distinguish between interoceptive accuracy (how precisely you can detect internal signals, such as your heartbeat) and interoceptive awareness (how well your confidence matches your accuracy), which can differ in the same person (Garfinkel et al., 2015).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Emerging science. Interoception is a real and important dimension of awareness, linked to emotion and mental health (Craig, 2009; Khalsa et al., 2018). Whether movement practices improve interoceptive accuracy or awareness is an open research question, and it has not been studied for the System’s tools.

Why mention interoception in a book about iron balls? Because practitioners of demanding physical arts often describe exactly this: a growing ability to feel what is happening inside, fatigue before failure, tension before injury, breath before panic. That sensitivity, whether or not it has been measured in this practice, is also a large part of what keeps a practitioner safe. Chapter 12’s stop rules depend on it.

Embodied mind

A broad movement in cognitive science, often called embodied cognition, argues that thinking is not something that happens only in the head, but is shaped by the body and its interactions with the world. A careful review distinguished six different claims made under this banner, from the modest (cognition is situated in real-world activity) to the bold (the environment is part of the cognitive system), and argued that some are far better supported than others (Wilson, 2002).

The modest versions are well-grounded and fit this book’s themes: perception and action are tightly coupled; skills are stored partly in the body’s patterns of movement; and the way we move shapes the way we perceive. A juggler literally sees motion differently after learning to juggle, as the brain studies in Chapter 6 suggest.

Can attention be trained?

The System claims that juggling trains predictive tracking of multiple objects and “multi-threat awareness.” What does the science of attention training say?

People can track several moving targets at once (Pylyshyn & Storm, 1988), and some training clearly improves aspects of visual attention. In a famous study, playing action video games improved performance on several measures of visual selective attention (Green & Bavelier, 2003). But the broader “brain training” literature urges caution: training reliably improves the trained tasks, sometimes improves closely related tasks, and rarely improves distant, everyday abilities (Simons et al., 2016).

So: attention is trainable, but often specifically. Juggling probably makes you better at attending to juggling-like situations. Whether it makes you more aware of threats in a crowded room has not been tested.

What “consciousness” means in this book

We can now say precisely what this book means when it speaks of an “upgrade in consciousness.”

It does not mean a proven change in the metaphysical nature of mind. Nothing in the scientific literature supports such a claim for juggling, bar work, or any physical practice.

It does mean the cultivation of capacities that science recognizes and, in several cases, has measured:

  • Presence: less mind-wandering, more absorption in what is actually happening (Killingsworth & Gilbert, 2010).
  • Flow: the experience of total, rewarding engagement, with reduced self-referential chatter (Ulrich et al., 2014; Harris, Vine, & Wilson, 2017).
  • Bodily awareness: proprioceptive and interoceptive sensitivity (Proske & Gandevia, 2012; Khalsa et al., 2018).
  • A changing brain: the plasticity that comes with learning new skills (Draganski et al., 2004).
  • A steadier mood: the well-documented effect of physical activity on anxiety and depression (Chapter 10).

If many people cultivated those capacities, more present, more absorbed, more at home in their bodies, more resilient, it is not unreasonable to call that a collective change in human awareness. It would be a modest revolution, built one practice session at a time. And it would be real.

Not a metaphysical leap, but a modest revolution: more present, more absorbed, more at home in the body, one session at a time.

Movement and Mood

Chapter 10

The body is not a vehicle for the mind. It is half of the conversation.

Of all the claims in this book, one rests on the broadest foundation of evidence: moving your body is good for your mind. It may be the single most important scientific finding behind any practice of physical training, and it applies to the System of Inevitability as much as to walking, dancing, or gardening.

The evidence, at scale

An overview of overviews. In 2023, Singh and colleagues pooled the results of 97 systematic reviews, covering 1,039 trials and 128,119 participants. Physical activity had medium-sized effects on symptoms of depression (median effect size −0.43), anxiety (−0.42), and psychological distress (−0.60), compared with usual care, across healthy adults, people with mental health disorders, and people with chronic disease. Higher-intensity activity was associated with greater improvement. The authors concluded that physical activity “should be a mainstay approach in the management of depression, anxiety and psychological distress” (Singh et al., 2023).

For clinical depression. In 2024, a network meta-analysis in the BMJ compared exercise types for people meeting clinical criteria for major depression, across 218 studies and 14,170 participants. Compared with active controls, walking or jogging, yoga, strength training, mixed aerobic exercise, and tai chi or qigong all produced moderate reductions in depression. Effects were proportional to the intensity prescribed, and strength training and yoga appeared to be the most acceptable to participants. The authors were also candid that confidence in the evidence was low or very low for most comparisons, because few studies had low risk of bias (Noetel et al., 2024).

For strength training specifically. A meta-analysis of 33 randomized trials involving 1,877 participants found that resistance exercise training was associated with a significant, moderate-sized reduction in depressive symptoms (Gordon et al., 2018).

At population scale. In a cross-sectional analysis of 1.2 million adults in the United States, people who exercised reported about 1.5 fewer days of poor mental health per month than otherwise similar people who did not, a difference of about 43% (Chekroud et al., 2018). Because this was a cross-sectional study, it cannot by itself show that exercise caused the difference, but it fits with the trial evidence above.

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established. Physical activity reduces symptoms of depression, anxiety, and psychological distress across many populations (Singh et al., 2023), and several forms of exercise, including strength training, are effective for clinical depression (Noetel et al., 2024; Gordon et al., 2018). The quality of individual trials varies, but the overall direction is consistent.

⚠ Caution

Exercise complements care; it does not replace it. If you are living with depression, anxiety, or another mental-health condition, exercise can be a powerful ally, but please work with a qualified professional. If you are in crisis or thinking about harming yourself, contact local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

Why might movement help?

Researchers have proposed many mechanisms, and probably several work together:

  • Biological. Exercise affects neurotrophic factors such as BDNF (Szuhany et al., 2015), stress-hormone systems, inflammation, and sleep.
  • Psychological. Exercise offers mastery experiences: concrete evidence that you can set a goal and achieve it. Albert Bandura’s theory of self-efficacy proposed that such mastery experiences are the most powerful source of a person’s belief in their own capability (Bandura, 1977).
  • Attentional. Absorbing physical activity interrupts rumination and draws attention into the present (Chapter 9).
  • Social. Exercise is often done with others, and social connection protects health (Chapter 11).

The particular gifts of a skill practice

Most exercise trials study walking, running, cycling, or lifting weights. A practice like the System of Inevitability is something different: it is skill training under load. It may combine several of the mechanisms above in unusual ways.

It is effortful, so it plausibly engages the biological benefits of exercise. It is absorbing, so it plausibly engages the attentional benefits of flow. And it offers mastery in an unusually vivid form. The day you first sustain a cascade for sixty seconds, or keep the ring centered through a full turn, you have unmistakable evidence that you can learn something hard. That is a mastery experience in exactly Bandura’s sense.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Reasonable inference, untested. That a skill-based, absorbing practice like juggling or ring-bar work combines the mood benefits of exercise with the attentional benefits of flow and the confidence benefits of mastery is a reasonable inference from the separate literatures. It has not been studied directly for these tools.

The day you first sustain a cascade for sixty seconds, you hold evidence in your hands that you can learn something hard.

Dose: how much is enough?

The evidence does not point to a single magic dose, but some themes recur:

  • Intensity matters. Both of the large reviews above found larger effects with higher intensity (Singh et al., 2023; Noetel et al., 2024). “Higher intensity” here means effortful, not reckless.
  • Strength work counts. Muscle-strengthening activities of roughly 30–60 minutes per week are associated with the largest reductions in mortality risk (Momma et al., 2022), and strength training reduces depressive symptoms (Gordon et al., 2018).
  • Consistency beats heroics. The benefits come from regular practice over weeks and months, which is also how skills and tissues adapt.

For most people, a few sessions a week of 20 to 45 minutes, combining skill work, strength work, and some walking, would sit comfortably within the evidence. Chapter 12 suggests how.

Movement as a daily return

There is a gentle idea hidden in the System’s phrase training method is just walking and turning. If the foundation of practice is walking, then practice is available every day, to almost everyone, in almost any condition. And walking, according to the largest network meta-analysis of exercise for depression yet published, is among the most effective forms of exercise for mood (Noetel et al., 2024).

You do not have to start with iron. You can start with a walk, and pay attention to the turning.

Part IV · The Spiral Outward

A spiral begins at a single point and widens with every turn.

From One Practitioner to Many

Chapter 11

“No hierarchy or competition required.” — System of Inevitability, public materials

The System of Inevitability was refined in solitude. I describe no teachers, no students, no ranks. And yet the hope behind this book is collective: that a practice like this, shared freely, might help many people become more present, more capable, and more connected. How does a solitary practice become a shared one without losing what makes it valuable?

Why solitude works, and where it stops

There is real wisdom in solitary practice. With no audience, there is no performance. With no ranks, there is no climbing. With no instructor, every insight has to be discovered in your own body. Many traditions, contemplative and martial, have honored long periods of solitary training.

Self-determination theory, one of the most extensively studied theories of human motivation, offers a way to understand why. Ryan and Deci (2000) proposed that people flourish, and sustain motivation, when three basic psychological needs are met: autonomy (the sense that your actions are your own), competence (the sense of growing mastery), and relatedness (the sense of connection to others). A meta-analysis of 73 health-related intervention studies found that interventions designed around these principles produced small-to-medium increases in motivation and health behaviour, and small improvements in physical and psychological health (Ntoumanis et al., 2021).

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established framework. Autonomy, competence, and relatedness support sustained motivation and wellbeing (Ryan & Deci, 2000). Interventions built on these principles produce modest but real benefits for health behaviour and wellbeing (Ntoumanis et al., 2021).

Solitary practice serves the first two needs superbly. It is entirely self-chosen, and it offers constant, honest evidence of growing skill. But it can leave the third need, relatedness, unmet. And as we will see, connection to others is not a luxury. It is one of the strongest influences on health ever measured.

The health of connection

In a landmark meta-analysis of 148 studies including 308,849 participants, Holt-Lunstad, Smith, and Layton (2010) found that people with stronger social relationships had a 50% greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up periods studied. The association held across age, sex, health status, and cause of death, and the authors concluded that the influence of social relationships on mortality is “comparable with well-established risk factors for mortality.”

● Evidence: well-established

Well-established association. Stronger social relationships are associated with substantially higher survival (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010).

Moving together

There is also evidence that moving in time with others does something special. A meta-analysis of 42 experimental studies with 4,327 participants found that synchronous movement, compared with non-synchronous control conditions, increased prosocial behaviour (a medium effect), perceived social bonding and social cognition (small-to-medium effects), and positive affect (a small effect) (Mogan, Fischer, & Bulbulia, 2017). Researchers studying music and dance have proposed that synchrony may blur the boundary between “self” and “other,” and may involve the brain’s endorphin system, as part of how human groups bond (Tarr, Launay, & Dunbar, 2014).

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

Suggestive. Moving in synchrony with others tends to increase cooperation, bonding, and positive mood (Mogan et al., 2017). The proposed mechanisms, such as self-other merging and endorphin release, are still being investigated (Tarr et al., 2014).

Juggling has a whole social world built around exactly this. Jugglers pass clubs and balls to one another in shared rhythms, gather in informal clubs and festivals, and teach strangers freely. A practice built on rhythm and continuous motion is naturally suited to being shared in time with others, even if each person trains alone most days.

A practice built on rhythm is naturally suited to being shared in time with others.

Community without hierarchy

So how might people share a practice like this without building the very ranks and gatekeeping the System rejects? Here are some suggestions. They are mine, offered in the spirit of the System's philosophy, not as its rules.

1. Share the tests, not the titles. Instead of belts, share simple, objective self-tests that anyone can run: cascade duration, grip strength, the CKCUEST (Chapter 12). These let people see their own progress and compare notes without anyone being ranked above anyone else.

2. Practice in parallel. Meet in a park or a garage and train side by side. Synchrony research suggests that simply moving in rhythm near others may foster connection.

3. Teach as a peer. Anyone who has learned the cascade can show someone else how to begin. Teaching is a form of practice, and no certificate is required to share what you know, as long as you are honest about what you don’t.

4. Keep a shared injury log. This is perhaps the most important and the least glamorous suggestion. A community that records what hurt, when, and at what load can learn collectively what no individual could learn alone. It turns anecdote into data.

5. Film your standards. A short video of a practitioner performing a pattern, with the load stated, is a standard that anyone can see and anyone can check. It replaces authority with evidence.

6. Separate the claims. Keep a clear line between what the practice does (measurable things like cascade time and grip), what it might do (plausible but untested benefits), and what practitioners believe or feel (philosophy and experience). Respect all three. Confuse none.

From practice to evidence

There is an exciting possibility here. The viability assessment that preceded this book identified what was missing for the System of Inevitability to become a transmissible system: a written progression, simple repeatable tests, filmed standards, and an injury log.

A community of practitioners, each running the same simple tests, filming their standards, and logging their injuries, could create exactly that, and openly. Over time, such a community could begin to answer questions no one has yet answered:

  • How do heavy-ball cascade times relate to grip strength?
  • How quickly do people progress from light to heavy tools, and what injuries occur along the way?
  • Do ring-bar practitioners improve on the CKCUEST?
  • Do practitioners with martial-arts experience notice any transfer, and can it be measured in partner drills?

None of that would be a formal clinical trial. But it would be honest, shared, and cumulative, which is the spirit of science. It might also, one day, give researchers enough reason to run a proper study.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

A suggestion, not a finding. Community-generated logs and filmed standards are not peer-reviewed evidence. They can, however, organize experience, reveal patterns, and generate questions worth testing properly.

Why this book is free

This book is released under a Creative Commons license that lets anyone copy, share, translate, and adapt it for non-commercial purposes, as long as they credit the sources and share their adaptations the same way.

That choice is not incidental. It follows from the logic of everything above. A practice without hierarchy should not be locked behind a paywall. A community that shares tests, logs, and standards needs shared materials. And if the hope is to help many people become more present and more capable, then the knowledge should move as freely as a ball passed from hand to hand.

The spiral outward

A spiral is a beautiful image for this. It begins at a single point, one person, alone, walking and turning, and with every revolution it widens. Each person who learns to juggle can teach another. Each practitioner who logs an honest result adds to what everyone knows. Each copy of this book given away may reach someone who needed it.

That is the most realistic and the most hopeful meaning of a collective “upgrade in consciousness”: not a sudden leap, but a widening spiral of people becoming more attentive, more capable, more honest about what they know, and more connected to one another.

The Safe Path: A Suggested Progression

Chapter 12

Heavy objects are honest teachers. They do not negotiate.

⚠ Caution

Read this first. Everything in this chapter is a suggestion compiled from general exercise science and common-sense safety practice. It is not the System of Inevitability’s official progression, because, as far as the public record shows, no written progression exists yet. It is not medical advice. Before starting any new training programme, and especially before using heavy implements, consult a physician, physiotherapist, or qualified strength coach, particularly if you are pregnant, have high blood pressure or a heart condition, osteoporosis, eye conditions, joint or spine problems, a previous injury, or are new to exercise. A standard pre-exercise screening questionnaire, such as the PAR-Q+, is a sensible place to begin.

This chapter is the bridge between inspiration and practice. Its purpose is to let almost anyone begin a version of this practice safely, to progress at a pace their tissues can follow, to know when to stop, and to measure whether anything is changing.

Five principles

1. Start far lighter than you think. The System’s tools, 6 lb balls and a 25 lb bar, rest on decades of adaptation. Your starting tools should be the ones the science actually used: ordinary juggling balls and a light stick. The juggling brain studies used ordinary balls (Draganski et al., 2004). The clubbell studies used 0.5–1 kg clubs (Walter et al., 2023).

2. Progress gradually, and change one thing at a time. Progressive overload, gradually increasing demand, is a foundational principle of resistance training (American College of Sports Medicine, 2009). Rapid spikes in load are a major contributor to soft-tissue injury (Gabbett, 2016). Increase one variable at a time: weight, or duration, or complexity, or height of throw. Never two at once.

3. Let tendons set the pace. Muscles adapt in weeks; tendons in months (Bohm et al., 2015; Magnusson & Kjaer, 2019). Feeling strong enough is not the same as being ready.

4. Age is not a barrier, but it is a factor. Resistance training is effective and appropriate for older adults when it is properly designed, progressed, and, ideally, supervised (Fragala et al., 2019). Older adults learn new motor skills (Voelcker-Rehage & Willimczik, 2006). They may need longer at each stage.

5. Measure, so you know. Self-directed practice needs a mirror. The three self-tests below are that mirror.

Set up a safe space

  • Clear the area. At least two metres around you, with no people, pets, glass, screens, or fragile objects. Nothing above you to hit with a bar.
  • Choose a forgiving surface. Grass, rubber mats, or thick carpet. A dropped iron ball on a hard floor can bounce unpredictably and will damage the floor.
  • Protect your feet. Wear sturdy closed-toe shoes once balls weigh more than about half a kilogram.
  • Never save a falling heavy ball. This is the most important rule of heavy juggling. When a heavy ball goes wrong, step back and let it fall. Lunging, reaching, or trying to catch it with a bent wrist or a finger is how injuries happen.
  • Keep throws below face height with any weighted ball. Low and controlled beats high and dramatic.
  • Train fresh. Do your most demanding skill work early in a session, not at the end when you are tired.

Warm up

A systematic review found that warming up improved performance in the large majority of outcomes studied, with little evidence of harm (Fradkin et al., 2010). A simple 8–10 minute warm-up suited to this practice:

  1. Walking and turning (2–3 min). Walk in a slow figure-eight, turning through the hips and shoulders. This is the System’s foundation.
  2. Joint circles (2 min). Wrists, elbows, shoulders, neck (gently), hips, knees, and ankles, in both directions.
  3. Grip wake-up (1 min). Open and close the hands; spread the fingers; gentle wrist flexion and extension.
  4. Light pattern rehearsal (2–3 min). One light ball tossed hand to hand, then two, then a light cascade. Or a broomstick held overhead, then at the chest, slowly turned.
  5. Breathing check. Breathe steadily. Avoid holding your breath during heavy holds or throws.

The suggested stages

The table below sets out a suggested progression. The weights and times are deliberately conservative. They are starting points to adjust with a professional, not prescriptions. Move to the next stage only when you meet the “ready to progress” standard for three consecutive sessions, with no pain flare the next day.

Stage Juggling Bar & ring Contact Ready to progress when…
0. Foundation (2–4 weeks) One ball, then two, hand to hand Broomstick held palms-down: overhead, chest, slow turns None Pain-free walking-and-turning warm-up; basic mobility
1. Light juggling (weeks to months) Ordinary juggling balls (~100–150 g). Cascade → 60 s Broomstick with a light ring (e.g. plastic bangle or rope loop); spin it centered, both directions Shadow striking, slow Cascade 60 s; ring centered 30 s each direction
2. Patterns Add Mills Mess, then Box, light balls; interleave patterns Light bar walks: forward, back, turning Light bag contact with wraps & gloves, short rounds Each pattern 30 s; ring centered while walking 30 s
3. Light load (months) Weighted balls ~0.5 kg (≈1 lb), low throws, short sets Light pipe or dowel ~1–2 kg with a light metal ring Moderate bag rounds Cascade 30 s at this weight, smooth catches, no wrist pain
4. Moderate load (many months) ~1–1.5 kg (≈2–3 lb) ~3–5 kg bar Dummy work introduced slowly Repeatable standards; stable grip and CKCUEST scores
5. Heavy load (adapted practitioners only, often years) Toward 2.7 kg (6 lb), only after long adaptation Toward 11 kg (25 lb); back-bend positions last and only if pain-free Full overlay work Filmed standards; clean injury log; professional input

Some notes on the table:

  • Durations are deliberately vague. Some people will spend weeks at a stage; others, months. Your tissues decide, not your calendar.
  • The 60-second cascade is the standard the Draganski study used for “skilled” juggling. It is a satisfying first milestone.
  • Stage 5 is optional. Most people can enjoy almost all the benefits discussed in this book, skill learning, flow, strength, mood, at Stages 1 to 4. There is no obligation to reach the System’s full loads.
  • Back-bend positions with a heavy bar load the lumbar spine in extension. Introduce them last, with a light bar, small ranges, and professional guidance.

Stop rules

These are rules, not suggestions. Stop the session, or stop the exercise, when any of the following occurs:

  1. Sharp, sudden, or localized pain, especially in the wrist, elbow, shoulder, or lower back.
  2. Pain that changes how you move, making you guard, limp, or alter technique.
  3. Pain above about 3 out of 10 during an exercise, or pain that is worse the next morning than before you trained.
  4. Numbness, tingling, or loss of grip in the hands or fingers.
  5. Dizziness, chest pain, unusual breathlessness, or palpitations. Stop and seek medical attention.
  6. Fatigue that degrades form. When catches get sloppy or the ring starts to wander constantly, the session is over. Practice tired, and you rehearse mistakes with heavy objects.
  7. Any blow to the head or face from a ball or bar, however minor it seems.
  8. Two dropped heavy balls in quick succession. Drop back to a lighter weight for the rest of the session.

If pain persists for more than a few days, or recurs every time you train, see a physiotherapist or physician. Do not train through it.

Specific injury cautions

  • Wrists and fingers. Heavy catches load the wrist in extension and the fingers in flexion. Catch with a soft, yielding hand moving downward with the ball. Never catch a heavy ball on straight fingers.
  • Elbows. Repetitive gripping can irritate the tendons at the inner and outer elbow. Rest at the first sign of persistent elbow pain.
  • Shoulders. Overhead bar work and heavy throwing stress the rotator cuff. Build shoulder capacity gradually; avoid pain at the top of the range.
  • Lower back. Avoid heavy bar work in back-bend until you have a long base of pain-free training at lighter loads.
  • Face and eyes. Keep throws low. Train in good light. Consider eye protection when working on new heavy patterns.
  • Feet. Wear sturdy shoes. Let dropped balls fall.
  • Blood pressure. Long, heavy holds with breath-holding raise blood pressure. Breathe throughout, and discuss heavy isometric holds with your doctor if you have hypertension or heart disease.

Three simple self-tests

Self-directed practice cannot tell improvement from hope without measurement. These three tests are simple, cheap, and repeatable. Test every four to six weeks, at the same time of day, after the same warm-up.

Test 1: Cascade duration

What it measures: juggling skill and consistency at a stated weight.

How: Using balls of a known weight, juggle a three-ball cascade for as long as you can, up to a ceiling you choose (for example 120 seconds). Record the time in seconds, or the number of catches, for your best of three attempts. Always record the ball weight, because a 60-second cascade with beanbags and a 60-second cascade with 1 kg balls are completely different achievements. Repeat for Mills Mess and Box if you practice them.

Test 2: Grip strength

What it measures: maximum hand-grip force, a strong marker of overall muscular health (Bohannon, 2019; Leong et al., 2015).

How: Use a hand-held grip dynamometer (they are inexpensive and widely available). Sit with your shoulder relaxed at your side, elbow bent at 90 degrees, forearm in neutral, wrist straight or slightly extended. Squeeze as hard as you can for about three seconds. Perform three trials on each hand, with rest between, and record the best. This is the standard approach used in clinical research and in the mace trial (Akaras et al., 2026).

Test 3: CKCUEST (Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test)

What it measures: upper-body stability, coordination, and endurance in a closed-chain (weight-bearing) position. It was one of the outcomes that improved in the mace trial (Akaras et al., 2026).

How (adapted from Goldbeck & Davies, 2000, and Tucci et al., 2014):

  1. Place two strips of tape on the floor, parallel, 91.4 cm (36 inches) apart.
  2. Get into a push-up position with one hand on each strip, body straight, feet about shoulder-width apart.
  3. On “go,” lift one hand, reach across and touch the other hand, return it to its line, then do the same with the other hand. Each touch counts as one.
  4. Continue for 15 seconds. Count the touches.
  5. Rest 45 seconds. Do one practice trial and then three measured trials, and record the average of the three.

In a reliability study, an improvement of at least three touches was needed to be considered a real change rather than measurement noise (Tucci et al., 2014).

⚠ Caution

CKCUEST caution. The test is demanding on the shoulders and wrists. Do not perform it if you have current shoulder or wrist pain. Beginners can practice the movement from a kneeling push-up position, but record that modification, because kneeling scores are not comparable with standard scores.

Optional: practice-specific measures

You may also wish to record:

  • Ring-centered time: seconds you can keep the ring spinning centered on the bar, in each direction, at a stated bar weight and position.
  • Bag rounds: number of rounds at a given duration with good structure and no hand or wrist pain.
  • Session feel: a simple 1–10 rating of effort, and a few words about mood and absorption. Over time, this can tell you how often you experience flow.

A printable log template is in Appendix A.

Keep an injury log

Every time something hurts beyond ordinary muscle soreness, write down: the date, what you were doing, the load, what hurt, how badly (0–10), and how long it lasted. Over months, patterns appear: a load that is too much, a pattern that strains a wrist, a time of day when you are careless. If practitioners ever share such logs, they will be the most valuable data this practice has.

A sample session (Stages 1–3)

Block Time Content
Warm-up 8–10 min Walking and turning, joint circles, grip wake-up, light toss
Skill 10–15 min Juggling patterns, interleaved (e.g. 2 min Cascade, 2 min Mills Mess, 2 min Box, repeat)
Bar 5–10 min Ring spin centered, both directions; positions overhead and chest; slow walking turns
Strength 5–10 min Simple grip and whole-body work appropriate to your level
Cool-down 3–5 min Slow walking; breathing; note your session in the log

Frequency. Short, frequent sessions favour skill learning (Shea et al., 2000), and sleep helps consolidate it (Walker et al., 2002). Three to five sessions a week of 20 to 45 minutes is a reasonable rhythm for many people. Allow at least one full rest day a week, and more when you increase load.

Building the habit

How long does it take for a practice to become automatic? In a study of 96 volunteers who chose a daily behaviour and repeated it in a consistent context, the time to reach 95% of maximum automaticity ranged from 18 to 254 days. Crucially, missing a single opportunity “did not materially affect the habit formation process” (Lally et al., 2010).

So: practice at the same time and place, link it to something you already do every day, and when you miss a day, simply begin again the next. The habit is built in the returning.

The habit is built in the returning.

A final word on safety

The deepest safety rule is not on any list. It is attention. The same quality of presence that makes this practice valuable, feeling the ball, the ring, the breath, the fatigue, is what keeps you safe. A practitioner who is truly paying attention knows when to stop.

And when in doubt, ask a professional. There is no belt for training alone through an injury.

A Closing Invitation

Chapter 13

“Training method is just walking and turning.”

We began with a single ball tossed from one hand to the other. Let us end there too.

Somewhere in your home there is probably something you could toss: a rolled pair of socks, an orange, a small beanbag. Pick it up. Toss it from hand to hand. Notice your eyes catching its arc, your other hand rising to meet it before you have decided to move it, the small give in your fingers as it lands. Notice that, for those few seconds, you are not anywhere else.

That is where this practice begins, and in a sense it is where it always stays.

What we have learned

The science gathered in this book does not prove that any particular tool will transform you. It shows something more modest and, in the end, more hopeful:

  • The adult brain changes when it learns, and learning to juggle was one of the first demonstrations of that in humans. It happens in young adults and in older adults. It fades if practice stops, and returns when practice resumes.
  • Skill is built through prediction, error, variety, outward attention, spacing, and sleep, and it is built specifically: we get best at what we practice.
  • The body adapts when asked patiently. Strength protects health. Balance and strength training prevent falls and injuries. Tendons are slow, and must be respected.
  • Attention is precious. A wandering mind tends to be an unhappy one; flow, the absorbed state that challenging skill practice invites, quiets the self-critical narrator and is rewarding in itself.
  • Movement lifts mood, reliably, across hundreds of trials.
  • Connection matters to survival, and moving together fosters it.

What remains unknown

We have also been honest about what we do not know:

  • No study has examined juggling heavy iron balls.
  • No study has examined a spinning ring on a steel bar.
  • No study has measured whether these tools transfer to fighting skill.
  • No study has measured whether they change awareness or consciousness in any lasting way.

Those are not failures of the practice. They are open questions, and open questions are invitations. Every practitioner who runs the simple tests in Chapter 12, films a standard, or keeps an honest injury log is helping to answer them.

The invitation

So here is the invitation, in four parts.

Begin. Pick up three soft balls, or a broomstick, or simply go for a walk and pay attention to the turning. Begin light. Begin today.

Pay attention. Let the ball’s arc, the ring’s centre, or the rhythm of your steps hold your attention. When your mind wanders, notice, and come back. That returning is the practice.

Measure. Keep a log. Time your cascade. Test your grip. Notice how you feel before and after. Let evidence, not hope, tell you what is changing.

Share. Teach someone the cascade. Train alongside a friend. Give this book away. A practice without hierarchy grows only by being shared.

Inevitability, again

There is one last meaning of “inevitable” worth keeping.

When a practice becomes part of your life, when you return to it day after day, through good weeks and bad, its effects become, in a quiet way, inevitable. Not because any single session is transformative, but because thousands of small sessions accumulate. The ball goes up and comes down. The ring turns. The foot falls and the next step follows. The catch becomes the throw.

That is the only kind of transformation this book can honestly promise. It is also, perhaps, the only kind that has ever really worked.

Walk. Turn. Catch what falls, and send it back up.

And then pass it on.

— with gratitude for the practice; to the researchers whose work is cited here, for the evidence; and to you, for what you will do with both.

A one-page summary of the main claims discussed in this book and the strength of evidence behind each.

Claim Strength Key sources
Learning to juggle (ordinary balls) changes adult brain structure in visual-motion regions, partly transiently ● Well-established, with methodological debate Draganski et al., 2004; Driemeyer et al., 2008; Scholz et al., 2009; Thomas & Baker, 2013
Older adults can learn juggling and show brain changes ● Well-established Boyke et al., 2008; Voelcker-Rehage & Willimczik, 2006

Far transfer from one trained skill to unrelated abilities ◐ Rare in well-controlled studies Sala & Gobet, 2017; Simons et al., 2016
Grip and muscular strength predict disability and mortality ● Well-established association Leong et al., 2015; Celis-Morales et al., 2018; Rantanen et al., 1999
Strength and balance training reduce injuries and falls ● Well-established Lauersen et al., 2014; Sherrington et al., 2019
Tendons adapt to progressive loading, slowly ● Well-established Bohm et al., 2015; Magnusson & Kjaer, 2019
Mace training improves grip, shoulder stability, CKCUEST ◐ One small RCT Akaras et al., 2026
Light club training improves shoulder strength and mobility ◐ Small RCTs Walter et al., 2023
Physical activity reduces depression and anxiety ● Well-established Singh et al., 2023; Noetel et al., 2024
Flow is associated with reduced self-referential brain activity ◐ Emerging Ulrich et al., 2014; Harris, Vine, & Wilson, 2017
Mindfulness programmes modestly improve anxiety, depression, pain ● Moderately established Goyal et al., 2014
Synchronous movement increases bonding and prosocial behaviour ◐ Suggestive Mogan et al., 2017
Heavy (6 lb) ball juggling produces the same brain effects as light juggling ○ Untested None
Spinning ring bar improves proprioception and tendon durability ○ Untested (plausible in part) None directly
These tools transfer to striking, clinch, or multi-threat awareness ○ Untested claim None
These practices upgrade consciousness in a metaphysical sense ○ Not a scientific claim None

● Well-established · ◐ Suggestive, emerging, or contested · ○ Untested, practitioner claim, or philosophy

Glossary

Autonomy — In self-determination theory, the sense that one’s actions are self-chosen. One of three basic psychological needs, with competence and relatedness.

BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) — A protein that supports the survival, growth, and plasticity of neurons. Levels rise with exercise.

Box — A three-ball juggling pattern in which two balls are thrown vertically at the sides while the third is passed horizontally between the hands, tracing a rectangle.

Cascade — The basic three-ball juggling pattern. Balls are thrown alternately from each hand to the other in crossing arcs, tracing a figure-eight.

CKCUEST (Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test) — A field test of upper-body stability. From a push-up position with hands 91.4 cm apart, the person alternately touches one hand with the other for 15 seconds.

Contextual interference — The finding that interleaving several skills in practice often hurts immediate performance but improves later retention and transfer.

Deliberate practice — Effortful, focused practice designed specifically to improve performance, usually with feedback.

Eccentric contraction — A muscle contraction in which the muscle lengthens under load, as when the arm “gives” to absorb a heavy catch.

Embodied cognition — A family of ideas holding that thinking is shaped by the body and its interaction with the environment.

External focus — Attention directed to the effect of a movement on the environment (e.g. the ball’s arc) rather than to the body’s movements.

Flow — A state of complete absorption in a challenging activity, with clear goals and immediate feedback, in which self-consciousness fades.

Fractional anisotropy (FA) — A measure from diffusion MRI reflecting how directionally organized water movement is in tissue; used as an index of white-matter microstructure.

Grey matter — Brain tissue rich in neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses.

hMT/V5 — A region of visual cortex specialized for perceiving motion. It showed grey-matter changes in the juggling studies.

Interoception — The sense of the body’s internal state: heartbeat, breath, hunger, temperature, visceral emotion.

Intraparietal sulcus (IPS) — A groove in the parietal lobe involved in linking visual information to action, including reaching and grasping.

Meta-analysis — A statistical method that combines the results of many studies to estimate an overall effect.

Mills Mess — A three-ball juggling pattern in which the forearms continuously cross and uncross, so that the balls appear to weave.

Mindfulness — Attention to present-moment experience, typically with openness and without judgment.

Neuroplasticity — The capacity of the nervous system to change its structure and function in response to experience.

Progressive overload — Gradually increasing training demand over time so the body continues to adapt.

Proprioception — The sense of the position, movement, and force of one’s own body, from receptors in muscles, tendons, joints, and skin.

Randomized controlled trial (RCT) — A study in which participants are randomly assigned to an intervention or a comparison group, the strongest common design for testing cause and effect.

Self-efficacy — A person’s belief in their capacity to succeed at a particular task. Strongly shaped by mastery experiences.

Specificity — The principle that training adaptations are specific to the type of practice performed; we get best at what we actually practice.

Spinning Ring Iron Bar — The System of Inevitability’s 5-ft, 25 lb stainless-steel bar, held palms-down, with a 6-in, 2 lb iron ring kept spinning and centered.

Stretch-shortening cycle — A pattern in which a muscle-tendon unit is stretched under load and immediately shortens, often recovering some stored elastic energy.

System of Inevitability — Emergent, free-form body expression with no set form, developed over more than twenty-five years by Cory Snell. Iron ball juggling, the spinning ring bar, the isometric push/pull with the ring, non-repetitive kinetic chaining on the bag, and work on the iron-armed dummy are its main expressions. It is a conceptual adjective that can be incorporated into any other system, anywhere, by anyone, and it claims no superiority. Its philosophy includes the line "training method is just walking and turning."

Systematic review — A structured review of all available studies on a question, using explicit methods to find and evaluate evidence.

Tendon stiffness — A tendon’s resistance to stretching under load; it increases with appropriate training.

Transfer — The extent to which practice of one skill improves performance on another. “Near transfer” is to similar tasks; “far transfer” is to dissimilar ones.

White matter — Brain tissue made largely of myelinated nerve fibres connecting brain regions.

About This Book

Title. Walking and Turning: Iron, Spirals, and the Science of a Practicing Mind — An evidence-based companion to the System of Inevitability.

Written by Cory Snell, creator of the System of Inevitability. First edition, November 2026.

Also in this series. Book 2: Wave and Return: The Bent Fist, the Figure-Eight, and the Science of a Restrained Hand, on the System of Inevitability’s striking: the bent (J) fist, whole-body wave energy, figure-eight motion, breath, safe progression, testing, and the ethics of restraint. Book 3: Shape and Choice: Everyday Geometry, Calm Presence, and the Science of a Choosing Mind, on the system’s everyday geometry, solitary training, calm presence, my own list of dangers, and the science of keeping choice inside automatic skill. Book 4: Lens and Lattice: Altered Perception, the Internal Arts, and the Science of a Curious Practice, a harm-reduction companion on practising the internal arts with curiosity in altered states, responsibly, and on the science of psilocybin, perception, touch, pattern finding, and integration. Book 5: Nucleus and Orbit: Atoms, Necessity, and the Science of an Interwoven Practice, on the system’s atomism, its 3-6-9 architecture, and its quantum language set beside the real science of atoms, necessity, chaos, the fractal body, and interdependence, tying the series together. The series continues. This book is Book 1 of the Companions to the System of Inevitability.

About this book. Written by Cory Snell, creator of the System of Inevitability. Descriptions of the System draw on my public statements of 30 and 31 July 2026 and on a project brief and viability assessment (October 2026). All progressions, tests, stop rules, and community suggestions in this book are mine, drawn from general exercise and motor-learning science.

Method. Every peer-reviewed study cited was checked against its Crossref record (authors, year, title, journal, volume, pages, DOI), and the specific findings reported were checked against the published abstracts or full texts. Numbers are reported as the original authors reported them. Where a claim is untested, the text says so. No quotations have been invented; the short quotations attributed to the System of Inevitability come from its public materials as summarized in the project brief.

Illustrations. All diagrams are original schematics created for this book. Figures of people are abstract and do not depict any real person. The plasticity diagram shows an illustrative shape, not actual data.

Typography. Set in EB Garamond and Cormorant Garamond, with Inter for labels.
